Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is better than computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans at assessing mural invasion in oesophageal and gastric cancer. Several studies have demonstrated the accuracy of staging with EUS is significantly higher than staging with CT or MRI.

Computed tomography (CT)
CT scanning is also useful and carried out for patients with oesophageal or gastric cancer. However, with regards to local staging (mural invasion), it is not as good as EUS.

Laparoscopy
Laparoscopy may be used in those with negative imaging before definitive therapy. For mural invasion, it is not useful.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
MRI scanning is useful to assess metastases and spread. As with CT, it is not as accurate as EUS.

Positron emission tomography (PET)
Positron emission tomography scanning is used for pre-operative staging and is more sensitive than CT in picking up distant metastases. EUS is still better than this for local staging.

stem: A 45-year-old female with a background of Sjogren's syndrome has been referred to the gastroenterology clinic due to impaired liver function tests. She is complaining of fatigue and pruritus which has been progressive over the last 3 months. On examination, her abdomen is soft, non-tender and without any organomegaly. Her laboratory investigations are as follows: Hb 110 g/L (115 - 160) Platelets 340 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 10 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Bilirubin 30 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 200 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 60 u/L (3 - 40) Î³GT 150 u/L (8 - 60) Albumin 37 g/L (35 - 50) AMA positive What is the first-line treatment to prevent progression of her liver disease?
explanation:
Ursodeoxycholic acid
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medication for primary biliary cholangitis to slow disease progression. Primary biliary cholangitis (previously referred to as primary biliary cirrhosis) is a chronic liver disorder typically seen in middle-aged females and is usually associated with other autoimmune diseases such as Sjogren's syndrome. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA) M2 subtype are present in 98% of patients and are highly specific. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line treatment that slows disease progression and improves symptoms.

Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine can be used to relieve pruritus but does not affect disease progression.

Liver transplantation
Liver transplantation is an option in decompensated liver disease (e.g. if bilirubin > 100).

Fat-soluble vitamins
Fat-soluble vitamins can be supplemented but are not a first-line treatment.

Methotrexate
Methotrexate is not considered a treatment option for primary biliary cholangitis, in fact, it should be avoided in hepatic impairment due to dose-related toxicity.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with several weeks of right-sided abdominal pain. He has recently migrated from Turkey and has no significant past medical history. On examination, the abdomen is tender in the upper right quadrant. Significant hepatomegaly is evident. An urgent ultrasound scan is requested: Liver ultrasound Multiseptated, multivesicular cyst - several daughter cysts present. Thin-walled, approximately 7cm diameter overall. What is the definitive treatment option for this condition?
explanation:
Surgery
Surgery is the mainstay of treatment for hydatid cysts. This patient's presentation and imaging findings are suggestive of a hydatid cyst. These occur due to infection due to the tapeworm parasite Echinococcus granulosus, most commonly in the Mediterranean and Middle East. An outer fibrous capsule forms, containing 'daughter' cysts as seen here. Most commonly, hydatid cysts form in the liver. Definitive treatment for the condition involves surgery to excise the cyst, ensuring not to rupture the cyst walls during the process. Concurrent treatment with antiparasitic medication, such as albendazole, takes place preoperatively and postoperatively. However, this is not the definitive treatment option for the condition - surgery is necessary.

Albendazole
Albendazole may be used in conjunction with surgery, as it can help prevent recurrence and manage the infection preoperatively and postoperatively. However, it is not the definitive treatment option for the condition - surgery is necessary.

Dexamethasone
Dexamethasone may be used in the management of allergic reactions in echinococcosis, especially following cyst rupture. It may also be administered as an adjunct to decrease perilesional oedema resulting from an intracranial hydatid cyst. The evidence supporting its use for oedema in hepatic hydatid cysts, however, is lacking. The definitive option here remains surgery.

Praziquantel
Praziquantel may be used in conjunction with albendazole, as some studies show the combination is more effective than albendazole monotherapy. These drugs, however, are used alongside surgery, not instead of it.

Puncture, aspiration, injection and reaspiration (PAIR)
PAIR is incorrect. This procedure may be suitable for patients with a simpler hydatid cyst (a unilocular cyst without 'daughter' cysts). However, as this patient's cyst is multiseptated, surgery is more appropriate.

stem: A 48-year-old man is admitted with a one-week history of jaundice and abdominal discomfort. He drinks 100 units of alcohol per week. On examination, he is jaundiced with tender hepatomegaly and shifting dullness. He is alert but confused. There are no signs of active infection or gastrointestinal bleeding. His blood results are shown. Bilirubin 250 µmol/L (3 - 20) ALT 85 IU/L (10 - 50) AST 210 IU/L (10 - 40) ALP 220 IU/L (30 - 130) Albumin 26 g/L (35 - 50) Prothrombin time 20 seconds (11 - 15) Creatinine 110 µmol/L (60 - 110) Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Prednisolone
Corticosteroids are used in the management of severe alcoholic hepatitis. This patient presents with a clinical picture consistent with severe alcoholic hepatitis. The diagnosis is suggested by the history of excessive alcohol intake, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, and the biochemical pattern of an AST:ALT ratio greater than 2. The severity of the condition, which dictates management, is assessed using prognostic scores such as Maddrey's Discriminant Function (DF) or the Glasgow Alcoholic Hepatitis Score. A Maddrey's DF >32 indicates severe disease with high short-term mortality. This score is calculated using the prothrombin time and bilirubin level. Given the significantly prolonged prothrombin time (20s) and markedly elevated bilirubin (250 µmol/L), this patient's score would be well above 32. In patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis and no contraindications, corticosteroids (typically oral prednisolone) are the mainstay of treatment. They have been shown to reduce 28-day mortality by suppressing the intense hepatic inflammation. The scenario specifically states there are no signs of active infection or GI bleeding, which are key contraindications.

Intravenous human albumin solution
Intravenous human albumin solution is not the most appropriate next step. Human albumin solution has specific indications in patients with decompensated liver disease, such as in the management of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), hepatorenal syndrome (HRS), or to prevent circulatory dysfunction following large-volume paracentesis. While this patient has ascites ('shifting dullness'), there is no indication for albumin at this point. It does not treat the underlying hepatic inflammation driving the alcoholic hepatitis.

N-acetylcysteine
N-acetylcysteine is incorrect. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is the specific antidote for paracetamol-induced acute liver failure. While there is some evidence for its use as an adjunctive therapy alongside corticosteroids in severe alcoholic hepatitis to reduce the risk of infection and hepatorenal syndrome, it is not the primary, first-line treatment for the underlying inflammatory condition. The definitive management to improve short-term survival is with corticosteroids.

Pentoxifylline
Pentoxifylline is not the correct choice. This agent was previously considered an alternative treatment for severe alcoholic hepatitis, particularly in patients with contraindications to corticosteroids. However, the large, multicentre STOPAH trial (2015) demonstrated that pentoxifylline, either alone or in combination with prednisolone, did not improve survival at 28 days, 90 days, or 1 year. Based on this high-quality evidence, UK guidelines no longer recommend its use in this context.

Supportive care only
Supportive care only would be insufficient for this patient. Supportive care is a crucial component of management for all patients with alcoholic hepatitis and includes complete alcohol abstinence, nutritional support (enteral feeding if necessary), and management of alcohol withdrawal. However, for patients with severe disease, as indicated by the prognostic markers in this scenario, supportive care alone is associated with a very high short-term mortality (around 30-50% at one month). Therefore, specific therapy with corticosteroids is indicated to improve survival.

stem: A 70-year-old is seen on the ward after originally being admitted for a chest infection requiring several courses of antibiotics. After the last course, the patient's respiratory symptoms improved however they developed diarrhoea with a stool sample testing positive for Clostridium difficile and so they were started on a course of oral vancomycin. Today is day 10 of the vancomycin but the patient still reports diarrhoea and abdominal cramps. Observations and investigations today are: Heart rate 102/min BP 130/80 mmHg Oxygen saturations 96% on air Temperature 38.1 oC WCC 15x109/L Abdominal x-ray Evidence of colitis 4.5-11 What treatment should be started now?
explanation:
Oral fidaxomicin
If C. difficile does not respond to first-line vancomycin, oral fidaxomicin should be used next, except in life-threatening infections. This patient has developed complications secondary to a Clostridium difficile infection most likely a result of extensive broad-spectrum antibiotic use. The patient has evidence of severe infection with a raised white cell count and evidence of colitis on imaging. First-line therapy for C. difficile is oral vancomycin for 10 days however if no improvement is seen then second-line therapy, in the form of oral fidaxomicin should be trialled.

Bezlotoxumab
Bezlotoxumab is a monoclonal antibody shown to target C. difficile toxin B, one of the main exotoxins produced by the bacteria causing intestinal damage and pseudomembranous colitis. Currently NICE do not support its use for the management of C. difficile as it is not cost-effective.

IV vancomycin
IV vancomycin does not have a clear role in the management of C. difficile infections with the oral form of the antibiotic used as first-line before escalating to other therapeutic agents.

Oral gentamicin
Oral gentamicin has very limited use for infection management in general with the IV formula used mainly for urinary infections and topical formula in eye and ear infections. Oral gentamicin has no role in the management of C. difficile.

Oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole
Oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole is reserved for third-line or life-threatening cases of C. difficile. This treatment regime should therefore only be used if oral fidaxomicin fails or the patient has features such as hypotension, ileus or toxic megacolon.

stem: A 43-year-old male attends the Emergency Department with acute abdominal pain. He recently attended his GP for a routine check-up and was found to have the following lipid profile. He does not take any regular medication: Cholesterol 6.6 mmol/l (<5.0) Triglycerides 21.4 mmol/l (<2.3) HDL 1.4 mmol/l (>1.0) LDL 4.4 mmol/l (<3.0) Cholesterol/HDL ratio 4.7 mmol/l (<3.5) In view of this result, what blood test would you like to request as part of his initial workup that could explain his abdominal pain?
explanation:
Amylase
In a patient with hypertriglyceridaemia and acute abdominal pain, an amylase should be checked to exclude acute pancreatitis.

stem: A 37-year-old lady is brought into the emergency department after being assaulted with a bottle. She reports being struck on the abdomen multiple times and reports pain across her entire abdomen. On clinical examination there is bruising across the abdomen however no distension, no guarding and no active sites of bleeding. Her initial observations as handed over from the paramedics are listed below: 30 mins ago 15 mins ago Now Heart rate 110/min 104/min 100/min Blood pressure 125/80mmHg 109/75mmHg 97/79mmHg Respiratory rate 18/min 14/min 14/min Temperature 37.2ºC 37.3ºC 37.3ºC She has been prescribed intravenous fluids and commenced on oxygen at a rate of 15L/min via a non-rebreathe mask. What is the single most appropriate initial investigation(s) to assess for the presence of free fluid in the abdomen and chest?
explanation:
FAST scan
FAST scans can be used to assess the presence of fluid in the abdomen and thorax. While CT imaging is useful in the assessment of free fluid in the abdomen and chest of trauma patients, the most appropriate initial investigation to conduct is a focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) scan. In the hands of a skilled practitioner, this can detect free fluid surrounding the kidneys, the spleen, the liver, bladder and pericardium. It is also possible to visualise all four chambers of the heart and to assess the hepatic vasculature. An extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST) can be conducted, which also assesses for pneumothorax. The sensitivity of a FAST detecting a pneumothorax is 40%, however is considered more sensitive than a supine chest radiograph at detecting pneumothoraces. FAST scans have replaced diagnostic peritoneal lavages as the investigation of choice for suspected haemoperitoneum.

CT abdomen and CT chest
While CT imaging is useful in the assessment of free fluid in the abdomen and chest of trauma patients, the most appropriate initial investigation to conduct is a focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) scan.

MRI abdomen and MRI chest
MRI imaging is less commonly used in patients presenting with traumatic injuries.

MRI abdomen and CT chest
MRI imaging is less commonly used in patients presenting with traumatic injuries.

Diagnostic peritoneal lavage
FAST scans have replaced diagnostic peritoneal lavages as the investigation of choice for suspected haemoperitoneum.

stem: A 75-year-old man was admitted 3 days ago after being found at home in his own faeces and urine. Prior to admission he was drinking a 70cl bottle of vodka per day but had not been eating for several weeks. This morning's blood tests showed that he was developing refeeding syndrome. K+ 2.3 mmol/L Mg2+ 0.46 mmol/L PO4- 0.51 mmol/L Which of the following is this man most at risk of developing as a consequence of refeeding syndrome?
explanation:
Torsades-des-pointes
Torsades-des-pointes secondary to hypomagnesaemia can result as a consequence of refeeding syndrome. Refeeding syndrome is characterised by electrolyte abnormalities including hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia. Severe hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia can lead to the development of torsades-des-pointes, a variant of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QT prolongation.

Atrial fibrillation
The other options are less likely to be precipitated by the electrolyte disturbances described in the question.

Ventricular fibrillation
The other options are less likely to be precipitated by the electrolyte disturbances described in the question.

Complete heart block
The other options are less likely to be precipitated by the electrolyte disturbances described in the question.

Left bundle branch block
The other options are less likely to be precipitated by the electrolyte disturbances described in the question.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with jaundice. This has progressively worsened over the past 4 weeks. On examination, her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no evidence of hepatosplenomegaly. You cannot identify any stigmata of chronic liver disease. Blood results are as follows: Bilirubin 84 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 832 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 224 u/L (3 - 40) Î³GT 962 u/L (8 - 60) Albumin 35 g/L (35 - 50) Ferritin 4842 µg/L (15 - 150) Hepatitis B core antigen Negative Hepatitis B core antibody Negative Hepatitis B surface antibody Positive Anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA) Strongly positive What treatment is indicated?
explanation:
Ursodeoxycholic acid
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medication for primary biliary cholangitis to slow disease progression. Ursodeoxycholic acid is correct. The clinical features and positive antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA) favour a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). Ursodeoxycholic acid is the main treatment for PBC. It can help prevent or delay liver damage in the majority of patients.

Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine can be used to treat symptomatic itch in PBC however it does not prevent disease progression.

Peginterferon alfa-2a
This drug can be used to treat hepatitis B. The hepatitis B serology suggests previous vaccination rather than active infection.

Prednisolone and azathioprine
This is the treatment choice for autoimmune hepatitis. This is a less likely diagnosis as this condition is often associated with anti-smooth muscle antibodies (SMA).

Venesection
Although the ferritin is significantly raised this is most certainly due to hepatic inflammation with subsequent release of ferritin from hepatocytes. Therefore haemochromatosis is a very unlikely diagnosis.

stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux presents with a several-month history of diarrhoea and weight loss. During the examination, he appears wasted and exhibits mild epigastric tenderness upon palpation. Multiple investigations, including a CT abdomen that revealed a suspicious mass, are conducted. Fasting gastrin levels were performed and found to be elevated, confirming the diagnosis. Where are the majority of these tumours typically located?
explanation:
First part of the duodenum
The majority of gastrinomas are found in the first part of the duodenum. This patient has presented with features of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, where increased levels of gastrin are secreted by gastrinomas. These neuroendocrine tumours primarily form in the first part of the duodenum due to it containing G cells, which naturally produce gastrin.

Ileum
Gastrinomas rarely develop in the ileum as this region lacks the specialised G cells responsible for natural gastrin production.

Jejunum
Gastrinomas rarely develop in the jejunum due to the unique distribution of gastrin-producing cells. G cells, responsible for producing gastrin, are primarily located in the antrum of the stomach and the duodenum. Consequently, gastrinomas tend to form in these regions or in the pancreas where G cells are also present. The absence of G cells in the jejunum makes it an uncommon site for gastrinoma development.

Pylorus section of the stomach
Gastrinomas rarely develop in the pylorus section of the stomach because gastrin-producing G cells are predominantly found in the antrum and duodenum. The pylorus, responsible for regulating the passage of food from the stomach to the small intestine, lacks these specialised cells.

Third part of the duodenum
Gastrinomas rarely develop in the third part of the duodenum as, being more distal in location, this area lacks the presence of gastrin-producing G cells where these neuroendocrine tumours primarily develop.

stem: A 73-year-old man has recently been admitted to hospital following a fall at home. He has a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, for which he takes ramipril, metformin and atorvastatin. His admission blood tests showed the following: Hb 102 g/L (135-180) Platelets 328 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 10.5 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) MCV 70 fl (80-100) Ferritin 12 ng/mL (20 - 230) He denies any change in bowel habit or weight loss and has not noticed any obvious bleeding elsewhere. On examination, he is noted to have an ejection systolic murmur that is loudest in the aortic area. Abdominal examination is normal and digital rectal examination does not reveal any abnormalities. What is the most likely cause of his anaemia from the list below?
explanation:
Angiodysplasia
Angiodysplasia is associated with aortic stenosis. This man has unexplained microcytic anaemia. There are a number of causes, of which angiodysplasia is the most likely option from the listed options. This is a common cause of iron deficiency anaemia and may present either with painless rectal bleeding or may be completely asymptomatic, as seen in this patient. It is thought to be associated with aortic stenosis, which is suggested by his ejection systolic murmur. Of course, it is essential to exclude more sinister pathologies such as colorectal cancer, hence further investigations would be required to confirm the cause of his anaemia.

Anaemia of chronic disease
Anaemia of chronic disease is a possibility given his chronic kidney disease, but this would typically cause normocytic anaemia with a ferritin level that is either normal or raised, hence this is an incorrect option.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Although it is a common cause of iron deficiency anaemia in patients who may not necessarily display any gastrointestinal symptoms, it is less commonly diagnosed for the first time in this age group and angiodysplasia would be the more likely cause.

Haemolysis from valve disease
Haemolytic anaemia would usually cause normocytic or macrocytic anaemia. Patients who have prosthetic heart valves can undergo haemolysis due to mechanical trauma to red blood cells, but there is no mention of this man having previous valve surgery, hence this answer is incorrect.

B12 deficiency due to metformin
Long-term metformin use is associated with B12 deficiency which can cause anaemia, but this usually results in macrocytosis, so would not be applicable to this patient.

stem: Which one of the following factors is most responsible for the increased rate of colorectal cancer in patients with ulcerative colitis?
options: Shared mutation in the HNPCC gene
explanation:
Chronic inflammation
The correct answer is chronic inflammation. Ulcerative colitis (UC) is associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer (CRC) primarily due to chronic inflammation of the colonic mucosa. The persistent inflammatory state leads to DNA damage, dysplasia, and ultimately malignant transformation through various molecular pathways including the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reactive oxygen species, and alterations in the p53 tumour suppressor gene. The risk increases with disease duration and extent of colonic involvement.

Shared mutation in the HNPCC gene
Shared mutation in the HNPCC gene is incorrect because hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), also known as Lynch syndrome, is a separate entity from UC-associated CRC. While both conditions increase CRC risk, they have different pathogenic mechanisms. HNPCC is caused by inherited mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes, whereas UC-associated CRC develops through inflammation-driven carcinogenesis.

Increased surveillance with colonoscopy
Increased surveillance with colonoscopy is incorrect because surveillance actually helps detect CRC earlier rather than causing it. In fact, regular colonoscopic surveillance is recommended for UC patients to monitor for dysplasia and early cancer detection, particularly after 8-10 years of disease duration.

Increased susceptibility to bacterial gastroenteritis
Increased susceptibility to bacterial gastroenteritis is incorrect because while UC patients may be more susceptible to certain gastrointestinal infections, this is not the primary mechanism for increased CRC risk. The relationship between bacterial infections and UC flares is complex, but it does not directly drive carcinogenesis.

Prolonged immunosuppression
Prolonged immunosuppression is incorrect because although many UC patients receive immunosuppressive therapy, this is not the main factor increasing CRC risk. While immunosuppression may slightly increase the risk of certain malignancies, the chronic inflammation itself is far more significant in promoting colorectal carcinogenesis in UC patients.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with abdominal pain and diarrhoea. She has no past medical history other than depression for which she takes citalopram. She smokes 20 cigarettes/day and drinks 20 units of alcohol per week. Ileocolonoscopy shows features consistent with Crohn's disease and she is treated successfully with glucocorticoid therapy. Which one of the following is the most important intervention to reduce the chance of further episodes?
explanation:
Stop smoking
The correct answer in this case is Stop smoking. Smoking cessation is the most important intervention to reduce the chance of further episodes of Crohn's disease. Studies have shown that smoking is a significant risk factor for developing Crohn's disease, and it has been associated with increased disease severity, higher rates of complications, and reduced response to treatment. Furthermore, quitting smoking has been shown to improve outcomes in patients with Crohn's disease.

Infliximab
Infliximab is an anti-TNFα agent used in the treatment of moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease. While it can be effective in inducing and maintaining remission, it is not considered first-line therapy for all patients with Crohn's disease. Infliximab would be considered if the patient had refractory or severe disease not responding to conventional treatments such as glucocorticoids or immunomodulators.

Stop drinking
Stop drinking may have some benefits for overall health but there is no strong evidence to suggest that alcohol consumption has a significant impact on the course of Crohn's disease. Reducing alcohol intake might help improve liver function and general well-being, but it would not have as profound an effect on reducing further episodes as stopping smoking.

Mesalazine
Mesalazine (also known as 5-aminosalicylic acid) is commonly used in the treatment of ulcerative colitis but has limited efficacy in preventing relapses in Crohn's disease. It may be used as an adjunct therapy for mild-to-moderate cases but would not be considered the most important intervention for reducing further episodes.

Budesonide
Budesonide is a glucocorticoid with high topical activity and low systemic bioavailability due to extensive first-pass metabolism. It can be used for induction of remission in mild-to-moderate ileocecal Crohn's disease but its role in maintenance therapy remains controversial. It is not considered the most important intervention for reducing further episodes in this patient.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 2-week history of diffuse itching, nausea, and generalised abdominal pain. She has a past medical history of epilepsy and rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, she appears jaundiced and has generalised abdominal tenderness, but no rebound or guarding. Her blood tests are below. Bilirubin 52 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 308 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 54 u/L (3 - 40) Albumin 42 g/L (35 - 50) What is the single most likely medication to be causing this picture?
explanation:
Oral contraceptive pill
The clinical scenario describes a classic cholestatic picture with hyperbilirubinemia, jaundice, and pruritus. The oral contraceptive pill can cause drug-induced cholestasis.

Methotrexate
Methotrexate is used as a disease-modifying agent and can cause fibrosis in the liver and lung and liver cirrhosis, rather than cholestasis.

Nitrofurantoin
Nitrofurantoin can work against gram-positive and gram-negative antibiotics and is often the first-line treatment for uncomplicated urinary tract infections. Unfortunately, a potential side effect is an acute hepatitis and hepatic failure, rather than cholestasis.

Phenytoin
Phenytoin and sodium valproate can both be used as anti-convulsant agents but can cause hepatocellular liver damage rather than cholestasis.

Sodium valproate
Phenytoin and sodium valproate can both be used as anti-convulsant agents but can cause hepatocellular liver damage rather than cholestasis.

stem: Which one of the following is most strongly associated with coeliac disease?
explanation:
HLA-DQ2
The correct answer is HLA-DQ2. Coeliac disease is a chronic small intestinal immune-mediated enteropathy precipitated by exposure to dietary gluten in genetically predisposed individuals. The major genetic factors are HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8, which are present in virtually all patients with coeliac disease. However, the presence of HLA-DQ2 is more strongly associated with the disease than any other factor, as it is found in up to 95% of patients with coeliac disease.

HLA A5
This option is incorrect because there's no such thing as HLA A5. Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) system or complex is a gene complex encoding the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins in humans. These cell-surface proteins are responsible for the regulation of the immune system. But within this system, there's no HLA A5.

HLA-DR2
This option is also not correct. While it's true that certain HLA types are associated with specific diseases, HLA-DR2 (now subdivided into HLA-DR15 and HLA-DR16) has been linked with multiple sclerosis and narcolepsy, but not coeliac disease.

HLA-DR4
This option again isn't right. The allele group HLA-DR4 has been associated with several autoimmune conditions including rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes mellitus, but it hasn't shown a strong association with coeliac disease.

HLA-B27
This last option isn't correct either. The presence of the human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27) is strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthropathies but not coeliac disease.

stem: A 45-year-old with known alcohol dependence presents with central abdominal pain and steatorrhoea progressively increasing over the last few months. The patient denies any clear trigger to his symptoms. The patient has been admitted several times in the past with acute pancreatitis. Blood tests are shown below. Hb 130g/L 130-180 WCC 5x109/L 4.5-11 Creatinine 100 µmol/L 53-106 AST 14 U/L 12-38 Bilirubin 16 µmol/L 2-17 Amylase 30 U/L 25-125 What is the preferred test to confirm the patient's suspected diagnosis?
explanation:
CT pancreas
CT pancreas is the preferred diagnostic test for chronic pancreatitis - looking for pancreatic calcification. This patient has a history of acute pancreatitis but has now presented with features and investigations in keeping with chronic pancreatitis. Chronic pancreatitis results from long-standing inflammation of the pancreas, commonly following several episodes of acute pancreatitis. Patients may present with a further episode of acute inflammation in a previously injured pancreas or with symptoms of persistent pain and malabsorption. The normal serum markers associated with acute presentations are often normal. CT pancreas is the diagnostic test of choice, detecting pancreatic calcification. CT has a higher sensitivity and specificity than other imaging modalities or serum tests and is readily available and therefore is the preferred diagnostic test.

Abdominal ultrasound
Abdominal ultrasound may show some signs in keeping with chronic pancreatitis such as calcification. However, it is not a suitably sensitive test when compared to CT.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is typically indicated to relieve biliary obstruction caused by stones, strictures or malignancy. It is not commonly used to diagnose chronic pancreatitis but is a well-recognised cause of acute pancreatitis. This procedure is also relatively timely, costly and invasive when compared to CT and therefore is not the diagnostic test of choice.

Faecal elastase
Faecal elastase testing is used for the detection of exocrine pancreatic dysfunction and not to diagnose chronic pancreatitis.

Urine amylase
Urine amylase may be used in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. A raised level indicates damage and some research indicates that it may be more sensitive at detecting chronic pancreatitis than serum testing. However, its sensitivity is low.

stem: A 48-year-old woman is admitted to the ward with jaundice of unknown cause. She noticed it in the mirror that morning. Some of her investigations are shown below: Hb 117 g/dL WCC 9.0 x 109/l Total bilirubin 124 umol/L LDH 75 U/L (100-250 U/L) Haptoglobin 45 mg/dL (30-200 mg/dL) ALP 324 umol/L AST 26 iu/l Examination of the abdomen reveals a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant and she has yellow discoloration of the sclera and skin. There are no other positive findings. Urine dipstick analysis shows high levels of conjugated bilirubin in the urine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cholangiocarcinoma
Cholangiocarcinoma is the correct answer. Cholangiocarcinoma is a cancer of ductal cells in the biliary tree. This can be painless and obstruct the bile ducts, causing jaundice with an obstructive picture (raised ALP, conjugated bilirubin in the urine).

Biliary colic
Biliary colic - This is not the most appropriate answer. Although this patient has an obstructive picture on her blood test results, biliary colic is, by definition, painful. A patient with biliary colic would not present in this way.

Haemolytic anaemia
Haemolytic anaemia - This is not the most appropriate answer. Haemolytic anaemia can present with jaundice; however, the blood tests results would be different to this patient - haptoglobin would be reduced and LDH significantly raised.

Gilbert's syndrome
Gilbert's syndrome - This is not the most appropriate answer. Gilbert's syndrome is generally a harmless condition which presents only with a raised bilirubin. ALP would not be raised in this condition.

Ascending cholangitis
Ascending cholangitis - This is not the most appropriate answer. Ascending cholangitis is an infective condition affecting the bile ducts. The typical triad of symptoms, known as Charcot's triad, is pain in the right upper quadrant, fever and jaundice. In addition, the white cell count would be raised.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents to the acute medical take with abnormal blood tests revealed by her GP. She has a long history of fatigue, and is also feeling generally unwell with malaise and non-specific arthralgia. She has also been investigated by her GP for dry eyes and mouth, and a generalised itch. On examination, she has excoriation marks over her arms, legs, and trunk. Otherwise she examines normally. Blood tests are shown below. Hb 135 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Bilirubin 30 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 145 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 35 u/L (3 - 40) Î³GT 90 u/L (8 - 60) Albumin 45 g/L (35 - 50) Anti-mitochondrial antibodies Positive Which of the following is the next most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Biliary ultrasound scan
Imaging is required before making a diagnosis of PBC to exclude extrahepatic biliary obstruction. This is a patient with dry eyes and mouth, fatigue, pruritis, and obstructive hyperbilirubinaemia. With positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies, the likely diagnosis is primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). The dry eyes and mouth are common in Sjogren's syndrome, which is commonly associated with PBC. It is vital to ensure that there is no extrahepatic cause of biliary obstruction prior to making this diagnosis, especially as the age commonly affected by PBC overlaps with those affected by cholangiocarcinoma and pancreatic malignancies. As such, an ultrasound scan would be a useful investigation.

Anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B antibodies
Anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B antibodies - are positive in Sjogren's syndrome. While these would be useful to confirm the diagnosis, it is more important to exclude extrahepatic biliary obstruction.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography - can be used if there remains uncertainty as to the diagnosis, but is invasive and not useful at this stage.

Liver biopsy
Liver biopsy - there is no need to conduct a liver biopsy in cases of PBC.

CT thorax, abdomen, and pelvis
CT thorax, abdomen, and pelvis - this would be a useful investigation if there was evidence of malignancy on other investigations, to stage the tumour or seek a primary in cases of metastatic infiltration. It would not be the next step in the management of this patient, however.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with small bowel obstruction secondary to adhesions from previous surgery. She has lost 15kg over the past 3 months due to abdominal pain and vomiting. Her BMI is 17 kg/m². She undergoes laparotomy and adhesiolysis. Postoperatively, she is commenced on total parenteral nutrition (TPN) via a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Three days later, she becomes confused and short of breath. On examination, she has a respiratory rate of 24 breaths/minute and oxygen saturations of 92% on room air. Her blood results are as follows: Na⁺ 136 mmol/L (135 - 145) K⁺ 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 6.2 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 78 µmol/L (55 - 120) Corrected Ca²⁺ 2.28 mmol/L (2.20 - 2.60) Phosphate 0.4 mmol/L (0.8 - 1.5) Magnesium 0.6 mmol/L (0.7 - 1.0) Glucose 7.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.5) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Refeeding syndrome
Refeeding syndrome is a recognised complication of TPN - the hallmark feature is hypophosphataemia. Refeeding syndrome is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario. This patient has several risk factors for refeeding syndrome: significant weight loss (15kg over 3 months), low BMI (17 kg/m²), and a period of minimal nutritional intake due to small bowel obstruction. When TPN was initiated, there was a sudden shift from a catabolic to an anabolic state, causing rapid intracellular movement of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium. The hallmark laboratory finding in refeeding syndrome is hypophosphataemia, which is evident in this patient's blood results (phosphate 0.4 mmol/L, significantly below the reference range of 0.8-1.5 mmol/L). Additionally, she has hypokalaemia (3.1 mmol/L) and hypomagnesaemia (0.6 mmol/L), which are also characteristic of refeeding syndrome. Her clinical presentation of confusion and respiratory distress is consistent with the neurological and cardiopulmonary manifestations of severe hypophosphataemia. Management would include correcting electrolyte abnormalities, temporarily reducing or stopping the TPN, and then gradually reintroducing nutrition with careful monitoring of electrolytes.

Catheter-related bloodstream infection
Catheter-related bloodstream infection is an important complication of TPN administration. However, this patient lacks the typical features of infection such as fever, rigors, or raised inflammatory markers. While confusion can occur in sepsis, the predominant biochemical abnormalities (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, and hypomagnesaemia) are more consistent with refeeding syndrome than infection. Additionally, catheter-related infections typically develop after a longer duration of central venous access than the three days described in this scenario.

Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism could explain the respiratory symptoms but would not account for the significant electrolyte abnormalities seen in this patient. While patients with recent surgery are at increased risk of venous thromboembolism, the combination of respiratory symptoms with profound hypophosphataemia and other electrolyte disturbances makes refeeding syndrome a more likely diagnosis. Pulmonary embolism would typically present with more specific respiratory symptoms such as pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis, which are not mentioned in this case.

Sepsis secondary to anastomotic leak
Sepsis secondary to anastomotic leak is an important postoperative complication following bowel surgery. However, the patient underwent adhesiolysis rather than bowel resection with anastomosis, making this diagnosis less likely. Additionally, anastomotic leaks typically present with abdominal pain, peritonism, and signs of systemic inflammation, which are not described in this case. The electrolyte abnormalities are more consistent with refeeding syndrome than sepsis from an intraabdominal source.

TPN-induced hyperglycaemia
TPN-induced hyperglycaemia is a common metabolic complication of TPN due to the high glucose content of the solution. However, this patient's glucose level is only mildly elevated at 7.2 mmol/L, which is unlikely to cause the described symptoms. Hyperglycaemia alone would not explain the profound hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, and hypomagnesaemia seen in this case. While glucose intolerance can occur during refeeding, it is not the primary issue in this scenario.

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with symptoms consistent with coeliac disease. Which one of the following tests should be used first-line when screening patients for coeliac disease?
explanation:
Tissue transglutaminase antibodies
Tissue transglutaminase antibodies (TTG) are the recommended firstline serological test for screening patients with suspected coeliac disease according to NICE guidelines. TTG antibodies have high sensitivity (around 93-97%) and specificity (around 95-99%) for coeliac disease, making them an excellent initial screening tool. These antibodies are produced when the immune system reacts to the tissue transglutaminase enzyme, which modifies gluten peptides in the small intestine, making them more immunogenic in susceptible individuals. TTG testing is widely available, relatively inexpensive, and has good reproducibility between laboratories. It's important to note that patients should be on a gluten-containing diet for at least 6 weeks prior to testing to avoid false negative results. If TTG is positive, further investigation with duodenal biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis.

Anti-endomyseal antibodies
Anti-endomyseal antibodies are highly specific for coeliac disease (specificity >99%) but are not recommended as the first-line test. They are more technically demanding, requiring indirect immunofluorescence on tissue substrates, making them more expensive and labour-intensive than TTG testing. Additionally, interpretation is subjective and requires experienced laboratory personnel. Anti-endomyseal antibody testing is typically used as a confirmatory test when TTG results are equivocal or to increase diagnostic certainty before proceeding to biopsy.

HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping is not appropriate as a first-line screening test for coeliac disease. While approximately 95% of coeliac patients carry HLA-DQ2 and most of the remainder carry HLA-DQ8, these genetic markers are also present in about 30-40% of the general population, most of whom will never develop coeliac disease. The main value of HLA typing is its negative predictive value – if a patient is negative for both HLA-DQ2 and DQ8, coeliac disease is highly unlikely. Therefore, HLA typing is more useful for excluding coeliac disease in specific situations, such as in patients already on a gluten-free diet or in first-degree relatives of coeliac patients, rather than as an initial screening tool.

Anti-gliadin antibodies
Anti-gliadin antibodies are no longer recommended for coeliac disease screening due to their lower sensitivity and specificity compared to TTG and endomyseal antibodies. These were among the first antibodies identified in coeliac disease and target gliadin, a component of gluten. However, they can be elevated in various other gastrointestinal disorders and even in some healthy individuals, leading to false positive results. Newer generation tests for deamidated gliadin peptide antibodies have improved performance but are still not recommended as first-line tests by NICE guidelines. Anti-gliadin antibodies have largely been replaced by TTG and endomyseal antibody testing in clinical practice.

Duodenal biopsy
Duodenal biopsy is considered the gold standard for diagnosing coeliac disease but is not appropriate as a first-line screening test. Biopsy is an invasive procedure requiring endoscopy, which carries risks and is more resource-intensive than serological testing. The typical histological findings in coeliac disease include villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. While biopsy is essential for confirming the diagnosis in patients with positive serology, it would be inappropriate and impractical to perform biopsies on all patients with suspected coeliac disease without first screening with serological tests.

stem: A 26-year-old man with a history of speech and behavioural problems presents with lethargy. On examination he is noted to have jaundiced sclera. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Wilson's disease
The most likely diagnosis for this 26-year-old man with a history of speech and behavioural problems, presenting with lethargy and jaundiced sclera, is Wilson's disease. Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by defective hepatic copper transport, resulting in copper accumulation throughout the body. The clinical manifestations are due to the toxic effects of excess copper and include hepatic, neurological, psychiatric and ocular (Kayser-Fleischer rings) symptoms. This patient's age, neuropsychiatric symptoms and jaundice (indicative of liver involvement) are typical features of Wilson's disease.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder that primarily affects males. It presents in infancy or early childhood with eczema, recurrent infections (due to immunodeficiency), and thrombocytopenia with small platelets leading to bleeding problems. This patient's age and lack of these characteristic features make Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome unlikely.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder causing excessive iron absorption from the diet. Over time, this leads to iron deposition in various organs causing damage. Symptoms typically include fatigue, joint pain, skin pigmentation ('bronze diabetes'), diabetes mellitus and liver disease (cirrhosis). However, these usually become apparent in middle age rather than at 26 years old as in our case.

Friedreich's ataxia
Friedreich's ataxia is a neurodegenerative disorder that typically presents before adolescence with progressive gait instability (ataxia), dysarthria, loss of deep tendon reflexes and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Although this condition can cause speech problems like our patient has, the absence of other key features makes it less likely.

Acute intermittent porphyria
Acute intermittent porphyria, part of a group of disorders called porphyrias which involve defects in heme synthesis. It might present with abdominal pain, neurologic symptoms and psychiatric disturbances. However, it does not typically cause jaundice or chronic neurological deficits such as those seen in this patient.

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with flushing, diarrhoea and abdominal discomfort. She says these symptoms have come on over the last few months and do not appear to be getting better. You decide to run some tests. 24-hour urine 5-HIAA is elevated confirming your diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome. A scan is undertaken which localises the neoplastic lesion to the jejunum. You start her on octreotide to calm her symptoms whilst she awaits surgery. What cardiac abnormalities are associated with this condition?
explanation:
Pulmonary stenosis and tricuspid insufficiency
Carcinoid syndrome can affect the right side of the heart. The valvular effects are tricuspid insufficiency and pulmonary stenosis. The syndrome is associated with right-sided valvular pathology. The most common pathology is tricuspid insufficiency and pulmonary stenosis. The best way to remember is the acronym 'TIPS'.

Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
HOCM is associated with inherited gene defects on the β-myosin heavy chain. This is not associated with carcinoid syndrome.

Acquired ventricular septal defect
Acquired VSD would be associated with an MI and not carcinoid syndrome.

Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection is associated with hypertension and connective tissue disorder.

Loeffler endocarditis
Loeffler endocarditis is endocarditis due to eosinophil proliferation in the heart. It is associated with helminthic infections and not carcinoid syndrome.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a distended, painful abdomen. He has a past medical of hypertension and alcohol dependence. He has recently returned from an extended trip to India. On examination, shifting dullness upon percussion of the abdomen is evident. A sample of ascitic fluid is obtained, and blood tests are performed, with the following result being calculated: Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) 16 g/L (< 11) What is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Alcoholic liver disease
Ascites: a high SAAG gradient (> 11g/L) indicates portal hypertension. The SAAG is a calculation used to help determine the cause of ascites. Under normal circumstances, the SAAG is < 11 g/L as serum oncotic pressure is counterbalanced by serum hydrostatic pressure. However, in several diseases, increased serum hydrostatic pressure causes more fluid to leave the circulation, leading to ascites. This increases the SAAG as serum albumin is concentrated. A high SAAG (> 11 g/L) indicates portal hypertension, either liver or non-liver related. Of the options listed, alcoholic liver disease is the most likely cause - as the liver becomes increasingly scarred due to alcohol, portal hypertension develops and leads to splanchnic vasodilation.

Nephrotic syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome is incorrect. Ascites caused by this syndrome is not associated with increased portal pressure, and thus the SAAG would be normal; it instead arises due to hypoalbuminaemia.

Pancreatitis
Pancreatitis is incorrect. Ascites due to pancreatitis is associated with a normal SAAG. This is relatively uncommon and usually arises from pancreatic pseudocyst leakage or ductal disruption.

Peritoneal carcinomatosis
Peritoneal carcinomatosis is incorrect. This peritoneal cancer is not associated with increased portal pressure, so the SAAG would be normal. Ascites arises in this condition due to increased permeability and thus secretion of peritoneal fluid, as well as obstructed reabsorption of this fluid.

Tuberculous peritonitis
Tuberculous peritonitis is incorrect. Although this is a valid concern, given the patient's recent extended trip to India, it is associated with normal-SAAG ascites, rather than a high gradient as seen here. Inflammation resulting from the infection leads to increased permeability and accumulation of peritoneal fluid.

stem: A 50-year-old lady is readmitted 3 days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones. She complains of frequent and uncontrollable diarrhoea. Abdominal examination eludes no features other than a laparoscopic scar. Her operation and initial recovery were unremarkable. In view of the history, what treatment is she likely to need?
explanation:
Cholestyramine
Post-cholecystectomy syndrome is a recognised complication of cholecystectomies. Typically symptoms of dyspepsia, vomiting, pain, flatulence and diarrhoea occur in up to 40% patients post surgery. The pathology behind the syndrome isn't completely clear, however there is some association with remnant stones and biliary injury. Pain is often due to sphincter of Oddi dysfunction and the development of surgical adhesions. Management is often difficult, but often involves a low-fat diet and the introduction of bile acid sequestrants, such as Cholestyramine, to bind the excess bile acids and thus preventing lower gastrointestinal signs.

Co-Amoxiclav
Antibiotics and pancreatic enzyme replacements play no part in management.

Pancreatin
Antibiotics and pancreatic enzyme replacements play no part in management.

Lansoprazole
Proton-pump inhibitors like Lansoprazole do play a role, if the patient is complaining of dyspeptic like symptoms.

stem: A 79-year-old woman has been admitted to the gastroenterology ward with abdominal pain. She has a past medical history of dyslipidaemia, hypertension, bronchiectasis and glaucoma. Her pain started two days ago but has been gradually becoming more severe. She has had a loss in appetite and diarrhoea. She is opening her bowels up to 5 times daily with some blood in the stool. On examination, she has a mild tachycardia of 108 beats per minute, a blood pressure of 107/62 mmHg and pyrexia of 37.9 ºC. Abdominal x-ray showed evidence of mucosal thickening of the large bowel with 'thumbprinting'. Due to concerns for ischaemic colitis a CT abdomen with contrast is arranged which confirms the diagnosis. Which part of the colon is most likely to have been affected?
explanation:
Splenic flexure
The splenic flexure is the most commonly affected site in ischaemic colitis. Given this woman's signs and symptoms along with 'thumbprinting' on her abdominal x-ray it is likely that she has ischaemic colitis. Ischaemic colitis most commonly affects 'watershed' areas. These are areas at the very edges of the territory supplied by particular vessels where there are fewer collateral vessels. At times of hypoperfusion, these sections of bowel are at an increased risk of ischaemia. The two most common 'watershed' areas in the large bowel are at the splenic flexure and the rectosigmoid junction. The splenic flexure is at the 'watershed' area of the superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric artery, whilst the rectosigmoid junction is at the boundary between the inferior mesenteric artery and hypogastric artery. Given the above options, splenic flexure is the correct answer.

stem: A 65-year-old obese man attends his GP for a routine blood test. His medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and gout. He consumes 20 units of alcohol per week and smokes five cigarettes daily. His medication includes metformin, gliclazide, and allopurinol, which he started 2 weeks ago. He does not take any over-the-counter medication. His blood tests reveal the following: Bilirubin 12 µmol/L (3 - 17) AST 104 U/L (0-40) ALP 45 U/L (30 - 100) ALT 120 U/L (3 - 40) γGT 62 U/L (8 - 60) Albumin 32 g/L (35 - 50) Hba1c 45mmol/mol Given the likely diagnosis, what would be the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Continue to observe LFT every 3 months
explanation:
Enhanced liver fibrosis blood test
The most likely diagnosis in this patient is non alcoholic fatty liver disease, given the patient's metabolic history with obesity and abnormal liver function tests. The elevated transaminases with normal ALP as seen in this case is typically seen in patients with non alcoholic fatty liver disease. Given this is a potentially new diagnosis, it would be appropriate to assess the extent of liver fibrosis through an enhanced liver fibrosis test in this patient to formulate appropriate management advice. The enhanced liver fibrosis is a non-invasive blood test that measures hyaluronic acid, procollagen III amino-terminal peptide, and tissue inhibitor of matrix metalloproteinase 1 to assess liver scarring and damage in chronic liver disease. It is typically performed first line due to the non invasive nature, cost effective and sensitivity in measuring active dynamic fibrosis providing insight into current fibrotic damage.

Continue to observe LFT every 3 months
Continue to observe LFT every 3 months may be appropriate if this patient were to have minimal fibrosis noted as a result of their diagnosis. However, at this point, as we do not know the extent of impact of the disease on this patient, it would be inappropriate to simply continue to observe without discussion regarding treatment to minimise the risk of future liver fibrosis.

Initiation of liraglutide
Initiation of liraglutide would not be appropriate currently. Although liraglutide may be used in the management of metabolic disease, particularly in improving weight loss, which serves as a key management step in non alcoholic fatty liver disease, it would be appropriate to trial non-pharmacological measures initially. Furthermore, this patient's hbA1c is also within the target, which would also make the initiation of liraglutide inappropriate currently.

Referral for gastric banding
Referral for gastric banding is typically reserved as a late-stage management step in patients with non alcoholic fatty liver disease following failure of non-pharmacological and pharmacological measures of control of weight loss and metabolic risk factors. As this is a new diagnosis for this patient, it would be appropriate to quantify the level of fibrosis initially and initiate non-pharmacological steps to manage weight loss and control of his metabolic factors before jumping to gastric banding.

Stop metformin and start pioglitazone
Stop metformin and start pioglitazone would be inappropriate in this case. There is no indication to stop metformin in this patient, particularly when his hbA1c control is good. Metformin is also found to be beneficial in the management of non alcoholic fatty liver disease.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a three-month history of jaundice, weight loss, and dark urine. He reports generalised fatigue and a loss of appetite but denies experiencing significant abdominal pain. On examination, scleral icterus is noted along with an epigastric mass. An abdominal ultrasound reveals dilatation of both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct, with no evidence of gallstones. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pancreatic head carcinoma
The 'double duct' sign may be seen in pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic head carcinoma is the most likely diagnosis because the 'double duct' sign—dilation of both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct—is strongly associated with this condition. The tumour typically compresses both ducts as it grows, leading to obstructive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and systemic symptoms such as weight loss and fatigue. The presence of an epigastric mass further supports the diagnosis, as it suggests an advanced lesion. This clinical presentation, including painless jaundice and systemic symptoms, is classic for pancreatic head carcinoma and is not characteristic of benign or less common conditions.

Ampullary carcinoma
Ampullary carcinoma is incorrect as it often presents with progressive jaundice accompanied by abdominal pain rather than the painless jaundice described here. Additionally, a palpable epigastric mass is uncommon in ampullary carcinoma, as these tumours are typically smaller. While systemic symptoms like weight loss can occur, the absence of intermittent jaundice and the presence of a palpable mass make pancreatic head carcinoma a more plausible diagnosis.

Cholangiocarcinoma
Cholangiocarcinoma is incorrect because although this malignancy of the bile duct can cause obstructive jaundice and bile duct dilation, it rarely results in concurrent pancreatic duct dilation, making the 'double duct' sign uncommon. Cholangiocarcinoma is more often associated with risk factors such as primary sclerosing cholangitis or liver fluke infection, which are not mentioned in this patient. Additionally, cholangiocarcinoma does not typically present with a palpable mass, further distinguishing it from pancreatic head carcinoma, which compresses both ducts and often produces systemic symptoms such as weight loss and fatigue.

Hepatocellular carcinoma
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is incorrect because it is primarily a malignancy of the liver and generally presents with right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, and elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels rather than the painless jaundice and 'double duct' sign seen in this case. While HCC can cause biliary obstruction through mass effect or invasion, this is less common and does not involve simultaneous pancreatic ductal dilation.

Primary duodenal adenocarcinoma
Primary duodenal adenocarcinoma is incorrect because although it is a rare malignancy that can present with obstructive jaundice and weight loss, it typically causes symptoms such as abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, or obstructive symptoms like vomiting. Duodenal adenocarcinoma does not commonly lead to concurrent pancreatic duct dilation, making the 'double duct' sign less likely. Furthermore, it is not strongly associated with the palpable mass and imaging findings described in this patient, distinguishing it from pancreatic head carcinoma, which remains the most plausible explanation.

stem: A patient with upper gastrointestinal symptoms tests positive for Helicobacter pylori following a urea breath test. Which one of the following conditions is most strongly associated Helicobacter pylori infection?
explanation:
Duodenal ulceration
Helicobacter pylori infection is also associated with both gastric adenocarcinoma and atrophic gastritis but the strongest association is with duodenal ulceration.

Gastric adenocarcinoma
Helicobacter pylori infection is associated with gastric adenocarcinoma, but the strongest association is with duodenal ulceration.

Atrophic gastritis
Helicobacter pylori infection is associated with atrophic gastritis, but the strongest association is with duodenal ulceration.

stem: A 55-year-old man is brought into the emergency department by the paramedics. He collapsed on the street suffering from a myocardial infarction and subsequently resuscitated following a cardiac arrest. Follow up blood tests are sent and the results show impaired liver function. He regularly has liver function tests as he is on a statin, and at his appointment last week they had been normal. There is nothing to note on examination and he is currently not complaining of any pain. ALT 1400 u/l Given this man's presentation, what is the most likely cause of his impaired liver function tests?
explanation:
Ischaemic hepatitis
This is a typical picture of ischemic hepatitis. Liver failure following cardiac arrest is often due to ischaemic hepatitis.

Hepatitis B
Hepatitis and chronic alcohol abuse would not cause such an acute rise in this man's liver function tests, and would most likely have been picked up by the GP.

Chronic alcohol abuse
Hepatitis and chronic alcohol abuse would not cause such an acute rise in this man's liver function tests, and would most likely have been picked up by the GP.

Budd-Chiari syndrome
Budd-Chiari syndrome characteristically presents with right upper quadrant pain associated with refractory ascites. And so this does not match his clinical picture.

Wilson's disease
Wilson's disease typically presents in teenagers or people in their twenties with neurological symptoms followed by liver failure. This does not match this patient's presentation.

stem: A 45-year-old man is referred to gastroenterology with dyspepsia and diarrhoea. He has been treated for presumed Helicobacter pylori infection by his general practitioner with no improvement in symptoms. He has no past medical history. He takes regular omeprazole 20mg once daily. He does not smoke or drink alcohol and works in IT. Abdominal examination reveals mild tenderness in the epigastrium with no guarding or rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are present. There is no organomegaly. Blood results are as follows: Hb 133 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 189 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 8.4 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 138 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 7.8 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 89 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 4 mg/L (< 5) Bilirubin 11 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 87 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 37 u/L (3 - 40) Î³GT 54 u/L (8 - 60) Albumin 37 g/L (35 - 50) Calcium 2.31 mmol/L (2.20 - 2.60) Parathyroid hormone 2.3 pmol/L (1.6-6.9) Prolactin 222 miU/L (<700) Stool MCS and faecal calprotectin are normal. An upper GI endoscopy is undertaken, which demonstrates numerous duodenal ulcers. A colonoscopy is normal. A CT chest, abdomen and pelvis is arranged, which demonstrates a single 1.5cm lesion in the distal duodenum. Given the likely diagnosis, which hormone level is likely to be abnormal?
explanation:
Gastrin
Gastrin increases H+ secretion by gastric parietal cells. This patient who presents with refractory dyspepsia, diarrhoea, multiple duodenal ulcerations and CT evidence of a possible primary malignancy is likely to have Zollinger-Ellinson syndrome caused by a gastrin-secreting tumour (gastrinoma). The multiple duodenal ulcers are caused by increased acid secretion by gastric parietal cells as a consequence of hypergastrinemia. Levels of serum gastrin, if measured, will be very elevated. It is sometimes associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (type 1) but normal levels of PTH, calcium and prolactin make this unlikely in this case.

Cholecystokinin
Cholecystokinin does not stimulate or inhibit acid secretion but rather causes the release of digestive enzymes from the pancreas and contraction of the gallbladder.

Secretin
Secretin, somatostatin and vasoactive intestinal peptide are all hormones that inhibit H+ secretion among their other effects and are therefore not the likely cause of numerous duodenal ulcers.

Somatostatin
Secretin, somatostatin and vasoactive intestinal peptide are all hormones that inhibit H+ secretion among their other effects and are therefore not the likely cause of numerous duodenal ulcers.

Vasoactive intestinal peptide
Secretin, somatostatin and vasoactive intestinal peptide are all hormones that inhibit H+ secretion among their other effects and are therefore not the likely cause of numerous duodenal ulcers.

stem: A 57-year-old man presents to the GP with several months of dysphagia, anorexia, weight loss and vomiting. He has a history of gastric oesophageal reflux disease and has smoked for many years. The GP urgently refers him to the hospital for an endoscopy - biopsy is taken from the visualised lesion, which reveals a malignant process. Which investigation is best for local staging?
explanation:
Endoscopic ultrasound
Oesophageal/Gastric Cancer - Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is better than CT or MRI in assessing mural invasion. From the above options, endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is best at assessing mural invasion of cancer for local staging. It is generally considered more accurate for this purpose than both computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

CT thorax and abdomen
CT scanning, whilst often performed as the first step, and useful for identifying the overt metastatic disease, is not considered as accurate as EUS for local staging.

Thoracoscopy and laparoscopy
Thoracoscopy and laparoscopy would be used to detect occult peritoneal disease, but not local staging.

MRI thorax and abdomen
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), similarly to CT, is useful as an initial scan - although not as cheap or as easily available as CT. MRI is not considered as accurate as EUS for local staging.

PET scan
Positron emission tomography may be used in those with negative laparoscopy, to assess peritoneal spread, but it is not the best choice for local staging.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to his GP with several months of fatigue and joint pain in his hands. He has no significant past medical history, but reports that his father developed diabetes in middle age. On examination, there is mild hepatomegaly and the skin appears slightly darker than expected for his ethnicity. His laboratory results are as follows: Ferritin 980 µg/L (30–400) Transferrin saturation 82% (15–50) ALT 56 IU/L (10–40) Which statement best describes the inheritance pattern of this condition?
explanation:
Autosomal recessive
Hereditary haemochromatosis most commonly results from homozygous mutations in the HFE gene on chromosome 6, inherited via an autosomal recessive pattern. Both parents must be carriers for a child to develop the disorder, which explains its higher prevalence in certain populations but absence in others despite carrier frequency.

Autosomal dominant
Autosomal dominant conditions require only one mutated allele to manifest disease and typically show vertical transmission through generations. Haemochromatosis does not display this pattern; family history may be present due to shared carrier status but not clear-cut dominant inheritance.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive disorders primarily affect males and are passed via carrier mothers to sons. Haemochromatosis affects both sexes and does not follow an X-linked pattern; it is linked to mutations on chromosome 6, which is autosomal.

Mitochondrial
Mitochondrial inheritance involves genes located on mitochondrial DNA, transmitted exclusively through maternal lines. The clinical features here do not fit with typical mitochondrial diseases, which often involve neuromuscular symptoms rather than iron overload states.

X-linked dominant
X-linked dominant inheritance would result in affected individuals of both sexes but with all daughters of affected males being affected, which does not match haemochromatosis epidemiology or genetic basis.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with six months of generalized itch. She has no past medical history. On examination, her abdomen is diffusely swollen and there is shifting dullness. There is xanthelasma. The neurological examination is normal. Blood tests: Bilirubin 54 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 321 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 88 u/L (3 - 40) Î³GT 888 u/L (8 - 60) Albumin 34 g/L (35 - 50) What blood result is expected to be elevated in this condition?
explanation:
IgM
Primary biliary cholangitis - the M rule IgM anti-Mitochondrial antibodies, M2 subtype Middle aged females IgM is correct. This middle-aged woman presents with itch along with clinical evidence of ascites (shifting dullness) and xanthelasma. Blood testing demonstrated deranged liver function tests with an obstructive pattern. Together, these findings suggest a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis, which is more common in middle-aged females. Raised IgM is a feature of this disease along with anti-mitochondrial antibodies.

Alpha1 anti-trypsin
Alpha1 anti-trypsin is incorrect. Alpha1 antitrypsin deficiency rather than excess can cause liver impairment and cirrhosis. This is therefore not the correct answer.

Copper
Copper is incorrect. There may be raised levels of copper in the blood in Wilson's disease. However, this disorder tends to cause a combination of neuropsychiatric and hepatic problems and presents at a younger age (usually < 20). The older age of this patient, xanthelasma, and the absence of neuropsychiatric features favour primary biliary cholangitis.

Epstein-barr virus DNA
Epstein-barr virus DNA is incorrect. EBV may cause acute hepatitis (or indeed hepatic failure) but it is less likely to cause chronic liver disease with an obstructive pattern. These findings favour primary biliary cholangitis.

IgG
IgG is incorrect. Raised IgG levels rather than IgM are more typical of autoimmune hepatitis. Xanthelasma is not stereotypical of this condition either. This answer is therefore incorrect.

stem: A 74-year-old woman inpatient complains of abdominal pain over the last 6 hours. The nurses report she has opened her bowels 7 times in the last 12 hours with watery diarrhoea. She has recently completed a course of intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed bacterial meningitis. Her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg, heart rate 105/min, temperature 38.7 ºC. Initial laboratory investigations are as follow: Hb 127 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 440 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 28.7 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) CRP 236 mg/L (< 5) An urgent stool sample is sent to the microbiology lab for culture and toxin analysis. What is the most appropriate antimicrobial treatment for this patient?
explanation:
Oral vancomycin and intravenous metronidazole
In life-threatening C. difficile infection treatment is with ORAL vancomycin and IV metronidazole. This patient is suffering from a life-threatening Clostridium difficile infection. She has recently received cephalosporin antibiotics, a known risk factor. She presents with characteristics signs and symptoms including abdominal pain, watery diarrhoea and a very high white cell count. The hypotension raises concern for life-threatening infection warranting aggressive antibiotic management. Public Health England (PHE) guidelines updated in 2019, recommend oral vancomycin and intravenous metronidazole as the treatment of choice in life-threatening Clostridium difficile infection.

Intravenous metronidazole
Intravenous metronidazole as monotherapy is not included in the guidance.

Intravenous vancomycin and intravenous metronidazole
Intravenous vancomycin and intravenous metronidazole are also not included in the PHE guidance though could be considered in a patient who may not absorb oral treatments well.

Intravenous vancomycin and oral metronidazole
Intravenous vancomycin and oral metronidazole are not suggested in the PHE guidance.

Observation only
Observation only would not be an appropriate antimicrobial strategy in a patient who is clinically septic. Even patients with confirmed mild Clostridium difficile infection, oral metronidazole is the treatment of choice.

stem: A 17-year-old female presents with a two-day history of right iliac fossa pain, nausea and loss of appetite. You suspect that she has acute appendicitis. Which scoring system, if sufficiently raised, could you use to lend support to your diagnosis?
explanation:
Alvarado score
The Alvarado score can be used to suggest the likelihood that a patient has acute appendicitis. It consists of eight different criteria (symptoms, signs and laboratory results) and divides patients into appendicitis unlikely, possible, probable and definite.

Child-Pugh score
The Child-Pugh score assesses prognosis in liver cirrhosis.

Glasgow score
The Glasgow score assesses severity of acute pancreatitis.

MELD score
The MELD score assesses the severity of end-stage liver disease.

Centor score
The Centor score assesses the likelihood that a pharyngitis is due to Streptococcus.

stem: A 22-year-old woman who is 34 weeks into her first pregnancy presents to the emergency department with severe epigastric pain and profuse vomiting. Her concerned partner tells you that she has no other significant past medical history and that she has attended all of her pregnancy checks. These have all been normal. On examination she is tender in the epigastrium. Her reflexes are mildly brisk and she does not have any clonus. Her blood pressure is 124/55 mmHg. You note that she is confused and point of care glucose monitoring reads 'low'. Her laboratory results return showing the following: Hb 110 g/l Na+ 132 mmol/l Bilirubin 94 µmol/l Platelets 123 * 109/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l ALP 173 u/l WBC 11 * 109/l Urea 8.5 mmol/l ALT 676 u/l Neuts 9.0 * 109/l Creatinine 98 µmol/l AST 590 u/l Lymphs 2.0 * 109/l CRP 15 mg/l Albumin 29 g/l INR 2.2 Urine PCR 5 Glucose 1.8 mmol/l A blood film shows no evidence of haemolysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) is a rare, potentially fatal complication that occurs in the third trimester or early postpartum period. Although the exact pathogenesis is unknown, this disease has been linked to an abnormality in foetal fatty acid metabolism. Early diagnosis of AFLP sometimes can be difficult because it shares features with other common conditions such as pre-eclampsia, viral hepatitis and cholestasis of pregnancy. However, a careful history and physical examination, in conjunction with compatible laboratory and imaging results, are often sufficient to make the diagnosis, and liver biopsy is rarely indicated. Supportive care and delivery of the baby are essential to optimal maternal-foetal outcomes and are the mainstay of treatment for AFLP.

stem: A 43-year-old woman is seen in the gastroenterology clinic with a four-month history of fatigue and intermittent right upper quadrant pain. Her wife noticed yellowing of her sclerae. The patient drinks two units of alcohol per week. The patient's GP requested an abdominal ultrasound which was unremarkable. Blood tests were sent: Hb 123 g/L (115 - 160) Platelets 242 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 5.6 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) APTT 30s (25-35s) PT 12s (10-14s) Bilirubin 30µmol/L (3-17) ALP 320u/L (30-100) ALT 32u/L (3-40) Î³GT 130u/L (8-60) IgA 2.3g/L (0.8-3.0) IgG 10.0g/L (6.0-16.0) IgM 6.0g/L (0.4-2.5) What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Ursodeoxycholic acid
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medication for primary biliary cholangitis to slow disease progression. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the correct answer. This patient has primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). Fatigue, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain are all in keeping with this diagnosis. The raised IgM is highly suggestive of PBC. Additionally, PBC tends to affect middle-aged women such as this patient. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the initial treatment for PBC. In PBC, there is autoimmune-mediated progressive destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts, resulting in chronic cholestasis. Ursodeoxycholic acid increases the transportation of intracellular bile acids across the liver cell and into the canaliculus, therefore reducing liver damage in patients with PBC.

Advice on alcohol cessation
Advice on alcohol cessation is the incorrect answer. Alcohol consumption of two units per week is unlikely to cause liver damage and there was no evidence of liver cirrhosis on the abdominal ultrasound. Given this patient has PBC, alcohol cessation might nonetheless be considered given this patient is at high risk for liver damage. However, alcohol cessation will not treat PBC and therefore ursodeoxycholic acid is the more appropriate answer.

Colestyramine
Colestyramine is the incorrect answer. Colestyramine is a bile-acid sequestrant that is useful to treat pruritus secondary to jaundice. This patient is not complaining of an itch and therefore colestyramine is not required at present - it would be reasonable to start should an itch develop. Colestyramine does not treat PBC.

Elective cholecystectomy
Elective cholecystectomy is the incorrect answer. Gallstones could explain intermittent right upper quadrant pain and an obstructing gallstone could cause jaundice. However, there is no evidence of gallstones or biliary dilatation on the abdominal ultrasound, making this very unlikely. Gallstones would not explain the raised IgM.

Liver transplant
Liver transplant is the incorrect answer. A liver transplant would be considered if PBC progresses to cirrhosis, or if there is clinical deterioration with no response to ursodeoxycholic acid. The patient's abdominal ultrasound showed no evidence of cirrhosis and the blood tests show no evidence of decompensated liver disease (normal platelets and clotting) - therefore a liver transplant would not be considered at present.

stem: A 65-year-old is seen on the ward after originally being admitted for a chest infection requiring several courses of antibiotics. After the last course, the patient's respiratory symptoms improved however she developed diarrhoea with a stool sample testing positive for Clostridium difficile and so she was started on a course of oral vancomycin. After completing a 10-day course she still reported diarrhoea and abdominal discomfort so treatment was changed to oral fidaxomicin.
