This is in contrast to the apoptosis seen in patients with mild cases of viral hepatitis, resulting in the possibility of regeneration and recovery of hepatocellular function.

stem: Which one of the following features is least associated with ulcerative colitis?
options: Inflammatory cell infiltrate in the lamina propria
Inflammation confined to the mucosa and submucosa
explanation:
Non-caseating granulomas
Non-caseating granulomas are not typically associated with ulcerative colitis. They are more commonly seen in Crohn's disease, another form of inflammatory bowel disease. Granulomas are clusters of immune cells that form in response to a persistent, non-eliminated threat such as bacteria, foreign substances or necrotic tissue. In the context of Crohn's disease, these granulomas are non-caseating meaning they do not have areas of necrosis.

Inflammatory cell infiltrate in the lamina propria
Inflammatory cell infiltrate in the lamina propria is incorrect because this is a common feature of ulcerative colitis. The lamina propria, which lies beneath the epithelium of the mucosa, becomes infiltrated with inflammatory cells such as neutrophils and lymphocytes during an active flare-up.

Pseudopolyps
Pseudopolyps is also incorrect as pseudopolyps are frequently observed in ulcerative colitis. They represent regenerative mucosal tissue following repeated cycles of inflammation and healing.

Depletion of goblet cells
Depletion of goblet cells is another incorrect option since it is often seen in ulcerative colitis. Goblet cells produce mucus which protects the lining of the colon from damage by stool and bacteria. In ulcerative colitis, chronic inflammation can lead to depletion of these protective cells.

Inflammation confined to the mucosa and submucosa
Inflammation confined to the mucosa and submucosa is not the least associated feature but rather characteristic of ulcerative colitis. Unlike Crohn's disease which can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and involves full-thickness (transmural) inflammation, ulcerative colitis typically only involves the colon and rectum with inflammation limited to the mucosa and submucosa layers.

stem: A 37-year-old woman who has a BMI of 44 kg/m^2 undergoes a Rouxen-Y gastric bypass. Of which vitamin/mineral is she most likely to require supplementation?
explanation:
Iron
The duodenum is the primary site of absorption for both iron and calcium. All gastric bypass operations bypass the duodenum. Nearly all menstruating women will therefore require iron supplementation.

stem: Which one of the following investigations is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease?
explanation:
24hr oesophageal pH monitoring
24hr oesophageal pH monitoring is gold standard investigation in GORD. The correct answer is 24hr oesophageal pH monitoring. This investigation is considered the gold standard for diagnosing gastrooesophageal reflux disease (GORD) because it allows for the direct measurement of acid exposure in the oesophagus over a 24-hour period. It provides quantitative data on the frequency and duration of acid reflux episodes, including those that do not cause symptoms, thus offering a highly sensitive and specific test for GORD.

Endoscopy
Endoscopy, while commonly used in the evaluation of GORD symptoms, is not as definitive as 24hr pH monitoring. Although it can identify complications such as oesophagitis or Barrett's oesophagus, it has limited sensitivity and specificity for GORD itself since many patients with typical reflux symptoms may have normal endoscopic findings.

Oesophageal manometry
Oesophageal manometry measures pressure changes within the oesophagus to assess its motor function. While this can provide useful information about peristalsis and lower oesophageal sphincter pressure, it does not directly measure acid exposure and hence is less accurate than 24hr pH monitoring for diagnosing GORD.

Barium swallow
A Barium swallow is an imaging study that can demonstrate anatomical abnormalities such as a hiatal hernia or severe oesophagitis but lacks sensitivity in detecting mild or moderate reflux disease. Furthermore, it cannot quantify acid exposure or correlate symptoms with reflux episodes.

CT thorax
Lastly, a CT thorax is not typically used in the diagnosis of GORD. It may incidentally show signs suggestive of GORD such as a hiatal hernia but lacks specificity and sensitivity compared to other investigations. Importantly, its use involves significant radiation exposure which makes it unsuitable for routine diagnostic purposes in this context.

stem: A 63-year-old man is admitted to hospital with several days of severe diarrhoea, fever, malaise and abdominal pain. 12 days prior, he started a course of levofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia. On examination, the abdomen is mildly tender and he has a fever of 38.3°C. A stool sample is taken and comes back positive for Clostridium difficile toxin. Oral metronidazole does not improve his symptoms, so he is switched to oral vancomycin. Going through his past medical history, the doctor notes that he has had several Clostridium difficile infections previously. Which of the following drugs may be beneficial in this patient's management?
explanation:
Bezlotoxumab
Bezlotoxumab is a monoclonal antibody which targets C. difficile toxin B. The correct answer here is bezlotoxumab - this is a relatively-new monoclonal antibody which binds to Clostridium difficile toxin B. It is licensed in Europe to reduce the risk of recurrence of C. diff infection in patients undergoing antibacterial treatment. It is not yet widely used.

Infliximab
Infliximab is an anti-tumour necrosis factor antibody, used to manage rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease.

Rituximab
Rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody, used in the management of rheumatoid arthritis and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

Suvratoxumab
Suvratoxumab is an anti-Staphylococcus aureus alpha toxin antibody, currently under investigation for the prevention of hospital-acquired pneumonia.

Trastuzumab
Trastuzumab, more commonly known by its brand name Herceptin, is a HER2/neu receptor antagonist, used in the management of metastatic breast cancer.

stem: A 23-year-old female with a history of diarrhoea and weight loss has a colonoscopy to investigate her symptoms. A biopsy is taken and reported as follows: Pigment laden macrophages What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Laxative abuse
The correct answer is Laxative abuse. The histological finding of pigment-laden macrophages in the colon, often referred to as 'pseudomelanosis coli', is indicative of chronic laxative use. Anthraquinone laxatives such as senna and cascara are culprits, leading to a brown-black discolouration of the colonic mucosa due to the accumulation of lipofuscin pigment in macrophages within the lamina propria.

Intestinal melanoma
Intestinal melanoma is incorrect because it is a rare malignancy that would present with more specific findings on biopsy, such as atypical melanocytes and the presence of melanin pigment within these cells. Melanomas can metastasize to the gastrointestinal tract but primary intestinal melanomas are extremely rare.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is also incorrect. This condition leads to iron overload and deposition throughout the body due to increased intestinal absorption. However, this does not typically cause diarrhoea or weight loss and the iron deposits would be found in parenchymal cells (like hepatocytes), not macrophages.

Ulcerative colitis
The option Ulcerative colitis is incorrect because it is an inflammatory bowel disease that would present with different histological findings such as crypt abscesses, goblet cell depletion and continuous inflammation starting from the rectum. Pigment-laden macrophages are not a feature of ulcerative colitis.

Colorectal cancer
Finally, Colorectal cancer is also incorrect. While colorectal cancer may present with symptoms like diarrhoea and weight loss, its histological findings would likely include dysplastic glandular structures or adenocarcinoma cells rather than pigment-laden macrophages.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a history of alcohol abuse undergoes an esophago-gastroduodenoscopy (OGD) following several episodes of unexplained epigastric pain. Several varices are identified in the lower oesophagus. It is decided that he is put on a prophylactic medication to reduce the risk of variceal bleeding. Which of the following medications would be most appropriate?
explanation:
Propranolol
Propranolol - This is the correct answer. A non-cardioselective β blocker (NSBB) is used for primary and secondary prevention of bleeding in oesophageal varices. They act by causing splanchnic vasoconstriction, reducing portal blood flow.

Omeprazole
Omeprazole - This is not the most appropriate answer. Omeprazole is used in the prevention and treatment of peptic ulcers.

Warfarin
Warfarin - This is not the most appropriate answer. Warfarin would increase the risk of bleeding.

Unfractionated heparin
Unfractionated heparin - This is not the most appropriate answer. Unfractionated heparin would increase the risk of bleeding.

Vasopressin
Vasopressin - This is not the most appropriate answer. The synthetic analogue of this medication, terlipressin, may be used to reduce acute variceal bleeding but not as a prophylactic agent.

stem: A patient is recovering in the gastroenterology ward after an upper gastrointestinal variceal bleed. He has ascites and jaundice as a result of a chronic hepatitis C infection. His routine blood tests come back showing impaired renal function. The results are shown below. They were normal 3 days ago when he was admitted. Urinalysis shows no protein or blood. Na+ 140 mmol/l K+ 3.8 mmol/l Urea 11.2 mmol/l Creatinine 302 µmol/l Given this man's presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Type-1 hepatorenal syndrome
Speed of onset can help to differentiate the type of hepatorenal syndrome. This question is asking about a patient currently admitted to hospital following an upper GI bleed. The patient is suffering from chronic liver failure and then goes onto develop renal failure. This is the typical history of hepatorenal syndrome. Hepatorenal syndrome is split into type 1 and 2. Type 1 is a rapid onset hepatorenal syndrome (less than two weeks). This typically occurs following an acute event such as an upper GI bleed. Therefore as his blood tests were normal 3 days ago this is type 1.

Renal calculi
Renal calculi would present with loin to groin pain as well as blood in the urine.

Focal segmental glomerulonephritis
In focal segmental glomerulonephritis, you would expect to see protein or blood in the urine and their absence helps to rule this out.

Type-2 hepatorenal syndrome
Type 2 is a more gradual decline in renal function and is generally associated with refractory ascites.

Minimal change glomerulonephritis
In minimal change glomerulonephritis, you would expect to see protein or blood in the urine and their absence helps to rule this out.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents for follow-up at the inflammatory bowel clinic. He has a long-standing history of ileal Crohn's disease, having been diagnosed when he was in his early 20's. Six months ago he was hospitalised with a severe flare, that failed to respond to medical therapy. Following an ileal resection with primary anastomosis at that point, his symptoms and inflammatory markers settled and he was discharged. Since then, he has had no problems with pain but continues to have diarrhoea, and is now opening his bowels 5 times per day. Recent investigations, including serum CRP, faecal elastase, and faecal calprotectin, have been normal. What is the most appropriate medication to reduce this patient's diarrhoea?
explanation:
Cholestyramine
Ongoing diarrhoea in Crohn's patient post-resection with normal CRP → cholestyramine. This is a man with ileal Crohn's disease who has diarrhoea post ileal resection. With a normal CRP and faecal calprotectin, this is likely secondary to bile acid malabsorption. In health, bile acids are secreted by the liver to aid in the emulsification of dietary lipids. Over 95% are subsequently reabsorbed in the terminal ileum. In patients with ileal Crohn's, especially those who have had a resection, this process is impaired. This results in bile salts progressing into the colon, where they stimulate increased water secretion and increased colonic mobility, giving rise to diarrhoea. Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant. It binds to bile acids within the GI tract and forms insoluble complexes which do not result in increased water secretion or colonic mobility. It is therefore the correct answer here.

Mesalazine
Mesalazine is a 5-ASA class drug that is used to reduce inflammation in inflammatory bowel disease, including ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Given the normal CRP and faecal calprotectin, it is unlikely to be of benefit here.

Pancreatic enzyme supplements
Pancreatic enzyme supplementation is used in cases of pancreatic insufficiency. Reduced pancreatic lipase results in increased lipid concentrations in excreted faeces, resulting in steatorrhoea. Given the lack of history of a cause of pancreatic insufficiency (e.g. chronic pancreatitis) and the normal faecal elastase, this will not help this man.

Ursodeoxycholic acid
Ursodeoxycholic acid is a bile acid that was first isolated from the bile of bears, and hence was named after Ursus, a genus of bears. It is used primarily in primary biliary cholangitis, where it may offer a mortality benefit. It would not be useful in this man, and may in fact worsen his symptoms.

Vedolizumab
Vedolizumab is a monoclonal antibody used in refractory Crohn's disease. It binds to integrin α4β7, resulting in gut-specific antiinflammatory activity. Given that there is no evidence of active Crohn's in this patient, this treatment would not likely be of any benefit.

stem: A 22-year-old man is investigated for weight loss and diarrhoea. A rectal biopsy is taken and reported as follows: Deep inflammatory infiltrate from the mucosa to the muscularis propria Numerous granulomata noted What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Crohn's disease
The most likely diagnosis in this case is Crohn's disease. Crohn's disease is a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus. The histological features described - deep inflammatory infiltrate from the mucosa to the muscularis propria and numerous granulomata - are characteristic of Crohn's disease. Unlike ulcerative colitis, which only involves the mucosal layer, Crohn's disease can involve all layers of the bowel wall, hence 'transmural' inflammation. Granulomas, although not present in every case, are also a key feature that helps differentiate Crohn's from other forms of IBD.

Rectal carcinoma-in-situ
Rectal carcinoma-in-situ is an unlikely diagnosis given the patient's age and symptoms. While rectal bleeding and changes in bowel habits may be seen with rectal cancer, it would not typically cause transmural inflammation or granuloma formation. Additionally, rectal carcinoma-insitu would usually be associated with dysplastic changes in the epithelium rather than deep inflammation.

Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis could theoretically cause granulomatous inflammation but it is much less common than Crohn's disease as a cause of chronic diarrhoea and weight loss in young adults in the UK. Furthermore, intestinal tuberculosis typically affects the ileocecal region more so than the rectum.

Laxative abuse
Laxative abuse can result in diarrhoea and weight loss but would not cause deep transmural inflammation or granulomas on biopsy. Instead, laxative abuse may lead to melanosis coli which is characterised by a brown-black discolouration of the colon due to lipofuscin deposition in macrophages within the lamina propria.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis, another form of IBD similar to Crohn's disease, primarily affects only the mucosal layer rather than all layers (transmural) as seen here. While ulcerative colitis can present with similar clinical features such as weight loss and diarrhoea, it does not typically produce granulomas on histology which makes it less likely in this scenario.

stem: A 58-year-old man attends the clinic with a 3-month history of profuse diarrhoea. He denies any melaena or fresh rectal bleeding. His weight is stable. Blood results are as follows: Hb 145 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 360 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 9.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 135 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 2.8 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 8.8 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 110 µmol/L (55 - 120) Bicarbonate 16 mmol/L (22 - 29) CRP 2 mg/L (< 5) A colonoscopy is arranged by the gastroenterologists: Colonoscopy Three large adenomas (>1cm) were identified in the descending colon, splenic flexure, and transverse colon What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Villous adenoma
Villous adenoma is correct. Most secretory villous adenomas of the colon cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with associated hypokalaemia because they produce large volumes of potassium, bicarbonate-rich fluid. The presence of adenomas, metabolic acidosis, and hypokalaemia favours this diagnosis.

Colorectal carcinoma
Colorectal carcinoma is incorrect. Although villous adenomas are premalignant, there is no evidence at the current time that they have transformed.

Familial adenomatous polyposis
Familial adenomatous polyposis is incorrect. Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is a rare inherited cancer predisposition syndrome characterised by hundreds to thousands of precancerous colorectal polyps (adenomatous polyps). If left untreated, affected individuals inevitably develop cancer of the colon and/or rectum at a relatively young age. In this case, only 3 polyps were identified making this an unlikely diagnosis.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is incorrect. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant genetic condition affecting around 1/50,000 and 1/200,000 individuals. Symptoms usually appear during the first decade of life and begin with spots of dark skin freckling (melanocytic macules) around the mouth, eyes, nostrils, and fingers as well as inside the mouth (oral mucosa) and around the anus (perianal). Multiple benign polyps called hamartomas also begin to grow in the gastrointestinal tract of affected individuals around that age. The presence of adenomas (as opposed to hamartomas) makes PJS an unlikely diagnosis.

Tubular adenoma
Tubular adenoma is incorrect. Tubular adenomas are rarely secretory and thus would not explain the biochemical results present in this case.

stem: A 66-year-old man has been referred to the upper gastrointestinal (UGI) cancer multidisciplinary team meeting (MDT) after a recent admission for dysphagia, reflux and weight loss. Barium swallow shows an apple core stricture of the distal oesophagus. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis shows a 2.5cm, circumferential mass in the distal third of the oesophagus which is concerning for malignancy. There was no evidence of lymphadenopathy or distant metastases. Which further investigation is the most appropriate to help stage this cancer?
explanation:
Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)
Oesophageal/Gastric Cancer - Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is better than CT or MRI in assessing mural invasion. If whole-body imaging has not shown any evidence of metastatic disease, EUS is the best investigation for tumour staging and can investigate for mural disease.

High-resolution CT scan
High-resolution CT is rarely required in cancer staging and is not beneficial in assessing for mural invasion.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
MRI helps assess for metastatic disease but does not aid in assessing for mural invasion.

Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (OGD)
OGD is the first-line for assessment of suspected oesophageal and gastric cancers, however is not able to assess for mural invasion and therefore is not the correct answer.

Positron emission tomography (PET) scan
PET scans are helpful in further identifying cancers and uptake in nodes and other tissues. It is, however, unhelpful in assessing for mural disease.

stem: A 54-year-old man with a long history of heartburn has an endoscopy to investigate his symptoms. A biopsy is taken from an abnormal area of mucosa in the lower oesophagus and reported as follows: Non-dysplastic columnar-lined oesophagus What is the most suitable management?
options: High-dose proton pump inhibitor and follow-up
explanation:
High-dose proton pump inhibitor and follow-up
The 2005 British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines state that high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy is first-line treatment in such patients.

Laser ablation
There is yet insufficient evidence to support the use of endoscopic ablation.

stem: Which one of the following foodstuffs contains the most calories per unit weight?
explanation:
Butter
The correct answer is Butter. Butter contains the most calories per unit weight amongst the options provided. This is because butter is primarily composed of fat, which provides approximately 9 calories per gram. This is significantly higher than carbohydrates and proteins, which both provide around 4 calories per gram. Therefore, foods that have a high fat content like butter will inherently contain more calories per unit weight.

White bread
White bread is incorrect as it mainly consists of carbohydrates with only minimal amounts of fats and proteins. As mentioned earlier, carbohydrates provide fewer calories compared to fats. Hence, white bread contains less caloric value compared to butter.

Pasta
Pasta predominantly comprises carbohydrates. Although pasta may have slightly more protein than white bread due to its wheat content, it still falls short in terms of caloric density when compared to butter.

Sugar
Sugar, while being a simple carbohydrate and providing quick energy release, also provides fewer calories per gram than fats. Thus, despite being calorie-dense for a carbohydrate foodstuff, sugar does not contain as many calories as butter.

Red meat
Red meat, although rich in proteins and containing some amount of fats too, does not surpass the caloric density of butter. Red meat generally provides around 7-8 calories per gram (depending on the cut), which is less than the 9 calories provided by fats found in butter.

stem: A 36-year-old man is reviewed in clinic. He has recently been started on mesalazine 400mg tds for ulcerative colitis. Which one of the following adverse effects is least likely to be attributable to mesalazine?
explanation:
Infertility
Sulphasalazine can cause oligospermia and infertility in men. Oligospermia is seen in patients taking sulphasalazine due to the sulphapyridine moiety, which is not present in mesalazine.

stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted with a 3-month history of generalised weakness and large-volume watery diarrhoea. He denies abdominal pain, fever, or blood in the stool. On examination, he has dry mucous membranes and reduced muscle power globally. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. Initial blood tests are performed. Na+ 136 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 2.4 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 8.9 mmol/L (2.5 - 7.8) Creatinine 110 µmol/L (60 - 120) CRP <5 mg/L (< 5) What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Villous adenoma
Diarrhoea + hypokalaemia → villous adenoma. Villous adenoma is the correct answer. This patient presents with a classic triad of chronic secretory diarrhoea, profound hypokalaemia, and dehydration (indicated by dry mucous membranes and a raised urea). Villous adenomas, particularly large ones (>2cm), are a rare but important cause of this presentation. They can secrete large volumes of potassium-rich mucus, leading to significant electrolyte depletion and volume loss. The patient's symptoms of generalised weakness and reduced muscle power are direct consequences of the severe hypokalaemia (2.4 mmol/L). The absence of inflammatory features (no fever, normal CRP, no blood in stool) and the chronic nature of the symptoms make an inflammatory or infectious cause less likely. The diagnosis is typically confirmed by colonoscopy, which would reveal the polyp, and management involves fluid and electrolyte resuscitation followed by endoscopic or surgical resection of the adenoma.

Laxative abuse
Laxative abuse is a very important differential diagnosis for chronic diarrhoea and hypokalaemia. It can produce an identical biochemical picture, often with a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. However, it is a diagnosis of exclusion and typically occurs in patients with underlying eating disorders or factitious illness, for which there is no evidence in this scenario. While it should always be considered in unexplained hypokalaemia with diarrhoea, a structural gastrointestinal cause like a villous adenoma must be ruled out first in an elderly patient with a new presentation.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is a form of inflammatory bowel disease that causes chronic diarrhoea. While severe diarrhoea can lead to hypokalaemia, the presentation is typically different. Ulcerative colitis characteristically causes bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain (tenesmus), and systemic signs of inflammation such as fever and a raised CRP. This patient's stool is watery and non-bloody, and his CRP is normal, making active ulcerative colitis a much less likely diagnosis.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is a cause of chronic diarrhoea due to malabsorption. While electrolyte disturbances can occur, the profound secretory diarrhoea leading to such severe hypokalaemia is not a typical feature. The diarrhoea in coeliac disease is more often steatorrhoea, and patients usually present with other signs of malabsorption, such as iron deficiency anaemia, weight loss, or other nutritional deficiencies, which are not described here. The primary mechanism is malabsorption rather than colonic secretion.

Infective colitis
Infective colitis is an unlikely diagnosis given the chronicity of the symptoms. A 3-month history of diarrhoea makes an acute bacterial or viral infection highly improbable. Chronic infections (e.g., Giardia, Cryptosporidium) are possible but are less likely to cause this degree of secretory diarrhoea and hypokalaemia. Furthermore, the absence of fever and a normal CRP argue against an ongoing infectious process, such as C. difficile colitis, which would typically present more acutely with systemic upset.

stem: A 64-year-old female patient is referred to the gastroenterology clinic with a 6-month history of recurrent epigastric pain, acid reflux unresponsive to antacids and a trial of proton-pump inhibitor. Gastroscopy is arranged which shows an ulcer in the descending duodenum and a tumour in the antrum of the stomach. Which type of cell this does this tumour originates from?
explanation:
G cells
Gastrin is produced by the G cells in the antrum of the stomach. The tumour in this patient is most likely a gastrinoma. Gastrinoma secretes excessive gastrin which causes increased HCL production, resulting in peptic ulcers. Gastrin is usually produced by the G cells in the antrum of the stomach.

S cells
S cells secrete secretin.

I cells
I cells secrete CCK.

D cells
D cells secrete somatostatin.

H cells
There is no such cell as H cell in the stomach.

stem: A 72-year-old man is referred to the sexual health clinic after presenting with perianal pain, bleeding and a palpable mass not in keeping with a haemorrhoid. On further questioning, the patient reports he has multiple male sexual partners and regularly has unprotected anal sex. A diagnosis of anal cancer is suspected and an anoscopic examination with biopsy is performed. Histology confirms the mass is a squamous cell carcinoma and based on its size it is staged at T3. What risk factor is the strongest risk for this patient's diagnosis?
options: Men who have sex with men
explanation:
HPV infection
HPV infection (especially HPV 16 subtype) is the strongest risk factor for anal cancer. Anal cancer is a relatively rare diagnosis, commoner in women, with most patients presenting in later life with symptoms of anal pain, bleeding and a lesion. There are several risk factors that increase a patient's risk of developing anal cancer but the rising levels of HPV infections have been attributed to the increased incidence of the malignancy. HPV infection is established as the strongest risk factor for anal cancer with approximately 80-85% of squamous cell carcinoma (which accounts for 80% of all anal cancers) being caused by the viral infection.

Being on immunosuppressive drugs
Being on immunosuppressive drugs has been shown to increase an individual's risk of anal cancer but like most other risk factors it is thought to be a result of the increased risk of HPV infection which drives the increased incidence of the malignancy.

HIV infection
HIV infection has been associated with anal cancer however the association is thought mainly to be a result of immunodepression caused by HIV increasing the risk of HPV infection and reducing the body's ability to keep the HPV infection under control.

Men who have sex with men
Men who have sex with men have a higher risk of anal cancer but again this is thought to be due to an increased risk of HPV infection.

Multiple sexual partners
Multiple sexual partners, if barrier protection is not used, can increase the risk of sexually transmitted diseases such as HPV which in turn is associated with anal cancer however this alone is a weaker risk factor than HPV infection.

stem: You are on a post-take ward round with your consultant and review a 48-year-old man who was admitted with sudden severe abdominal pain, confusion and pyrexia. He has a background of alcoholic cirrhosis and known ascites which is normally asymptomatic. An ascitic tap was done overnight which showed a neutrophil count of 375/mm³ and was sent for urgent microscopy & culture. What organism is most likely to grow from the ascitic tap?
explanation:
E. coli
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: most common organism found on ascitic fluid culture is E. coli E. coli is the most commonly grown organism.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is not correct, it is a cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis however it is not the most common.

Klebsiella
Klebsiella is not correct, it is a cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis however it is not the most common.

Streptococcus
Streptococcus is not correct, it is a cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis however it is not the most common.

Enterococcus
Enterococcus is not correct, is a cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis however it is not the most common.

stem: A 70-year-old man who is known to have atrial fibrillation presents with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. A diagnosis of ischaemic colitis is suspected. Which part of the colon is most likely to be affected?
explanation:
Splenic flexure
The splenic flexure is the most likely area to be affected by ischaemic colitis. The splenic flexure, also known as the left colic flexure, is one of the watershed areas of the colon. A watershed area refers to a region that receives dual blood supply from the end arteries and therefore it is more vulnerable to ischaemia when systemic perfusion decreases or there's vascular occlusion. In atrial fibrillation, embolisation can occur leading to occlusion of these end arteries and hence ischemia.

Hepatic flexure
The Hepatic flexure, also known as right colic flexure, is less likely to be affected by ischemia because it has a better blood supply compared with the splenic flexure. It is primarily supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). However, if SMA itself gets blocked then hepatic flexure could get involved but in comparison with splenic flexure, the incidence is lower.

Descending colon
The Descending colon has a rich blood supply from branches of Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA) making it less susceptible to ischemia than the splenic flexure.

Ascending colon
The Ascending colon, like hepatic flexure, primarily gets its blood supply from Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA). Hence it's less likely to be affected by ischemia unless SMA gets blocked.

Rectum
The Rectum has an abundant blood supply from both systemic and portal circulation via Superior Rectal Artery (from IMA), Middle Rectal Artery (from Internal Iliac Artery), and Inferior Rectal Artery (from Internal Pudendal Artery). Therefore, this makes rectum less prone to ischemia compared with splenic flexure.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a 4-week history of profuse diarrhoea. He denies blood or mucus. He is taking 8mg of loperamide four times per day. He underwent an ileocecal resection 6-weeks ago as part of his treatment for Crohn's disease. Blood results are as follows: Hb 132 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 162 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 7.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 136 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 7.8 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 92 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 2 mg/L (< 5) Stool results are as follows: Faecal elastase 440 ug/g Stool microscopy and culture Negative Stool virology Negative (>200) What treatment is indicated?
explanation:
Cholestyramine
Ongoing diarrhoea in Crohn's patient post-resection with normal CRP → cholestyramine. Cholestyramine is correct. The patient most likely has a diagnosis of bile acid malabsorption as a complication of the ileocecal resection. Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant with the potential to control diarrhoea induced by bile acid malabsorption.

Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is incorrect. This can be used to treat bacterial gastroenteritis, however, the stool culture is negative making this an unlikely diagnosis.

Octreotide
Octreotide is incorrect. Octreotide is a synthetic analogue of somatostatin used in palliative care to relieve symptoms associated with unresectable hormone-secreting tumours (for example carcinoid), intractable diarrhoea related to high output ileostomies or inoperable bowel obstruction in patients with cancer. Although it has the potential to be effective in this case, a trial of cholestyramine in this first instance would be preferable.

Pancreatic enzyme
Pancreatic enzyme is incorrect. These agents can be useful in pancreatic insufficiency. However, the normal faecal elastase, in this case, makes this a less likely diagnosis.

Rifaximin
Rifaximin is incorrect. This drug is useful for small bowel bacterial overgrowth. This condition presents with abdominal pain, belching, bloating, diarrhoea, and flatulence. Although it remains within the differential diagnosis, further investigations would be required (e.g. hydrogen breath test) prior to initiating rifaximin.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents with shortness-of-breath. He has a past history of aortic stenosis but is otherwise well. On examination he has a systolic murmur and a clear chest. Routine bloods are as follows: Hb 8.7 g/dl MCV 71 fl Plt 277 * 109/l WBC 6.4 * 109/l Which one of the following investigations is most likely to explain his anaemia?
explanation:
Colonoscopy
The correct answer is Colonoscopy. The patient's blood results show a microcytic anaemia (MCV < 80 fl), which is most commonly caused by iron deficiency. In the UK, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend that men and nonmenstruating women with iron deficiency anaemia should have a gastrointestinal investigation such as a colonoscopy to look for a source of bleeding, as this is the most common cause in these groups.

Renal biopsy
Renal biopsy is not the best choice because kidney disease can cause normocytic or sometimes macrocytic anaemia, but not typically microcytic anaemia. Additionally, renal disease would usually present with other symptoms or signs such as hypertension, oedema or abnormal renal function tests.

Duodenal biopsy
A Duodenal biopsy could potentially identify coeliac disease, which can lead to iron deficiency anaemia due to malabsorption. However, this is less likely than gastrointestinal bleeding to be the cause of iron deficiency in an elderly man without other symptoms suggestive of coeliac disease.

Gastroscopy
Gastroscopy could also identify a source of upper gastrointestinal bleeding leading to iron deficiency anaemia. However, colonoscopy would normally be chosen first in an older person because colorectal cancer is more common than gastric cancer in the UK.

Echocardiogram
An Echocardiogram may be useful in assessing his cardiac status given his history of aortic stenosis and presenting symptom of breathlessness. However, it would not directly explain his anaemia unless he had severe heart failure causing high-output cardiac failure leading to dilutional anaemia - but this is usually normocytic rather than microcytic.

stem: A 49-year-old woman who is known to have alcoholic liver disease is admitted to the ward following a decompensation. A diagnosis of grade II hepatic encephalopathy is made. She is confused and a screen looking for infection and other precipitants is performed. She is started on lactulose. What other medication may be used to prevent the hepatic encephalopathy if lactulose is ineffective?
explanation:
Rifaximin
Rifaximin is a non-absorbable antibiotic that acts within the gastrointestinal tract to reduce the production and absorption of ammonia, which is a key factor in the development of hepatic encephalopathy. It is used as an add-on therapy to lactulose when lactulose alone is insufficient in controlling hepatic encephalopathy. Rifaximin has been shown to be effective in reducing recurrence rates and improving cognitive function in patients with hepatic encephalopathy.

Neomycin
Neomycin was historically used as an alternative to lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy. However, it has fallen out of favor due to its nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, which can lead to renal impairment and hearing loss. Additionally, neomycin is less effective than rifaximin and has more side effects.

Senna
Senna is a stimulant laxative that increases bowel motility but does not specifically target ammonia production or absorption. While it may help alleviate constipation, it would not be effective in preventing hepatic encephalopathy.

Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that may be used in treating infections that could precipitate hepatic encephalopathy (such as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), but it does not have a direct effect on ammonia levels or the management of hepatic encephalopathy itself.

High-dose vitamin C
High-dose vitamin C has no proven role in the prevention or treatment of hepatic encephalopathy. While vitamin C has antioxidant properties and may have some general health benefits, there is no evidence supporting its use for this specific condition.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is referred to the gastroenterology outpatient department after a six-month history of weight loss and diarrhoea was noted by her mother. She has no past medical history. The examination was unremarkable. Her body mass index was 17 kg/m^2. A colonoscopy was undertaken and the biopsy demonstrated pigment-laden macrophages. No organisms were demonstrated. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Laxative abuse
Laxative abuse is correct. The biopsy demonstrates pigment-laden macrophages and this is consistent with laxative abuse. Notably, the mother raised concerns regarding her symptoms, suggesting that the patient herself was not forthcoming.

Crohn's disease
Crohn's disease is incorrect. This can cause weight loss and diarrhoea. However, at colonoscopy, you would expect transmural inflammation and granulomata in some cases. These are not present here. Pigment-laden macrophages would not be expected.

Irritable bowel syndrome
Irritable bowel syndrome is incorrect. Weight loss is not typically a feature of irritable bowel syndrome. Additionally, colonoscopy results are not typically different in patients with irritable bowel syndrome versus healthy controls. Microscopic colitis may be found in a small number of cases. Pigment-laden macrophages would not be expected.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. At colonoscopy, we would expect to find inflammation i.e. colitis. This is not mentioned in this case. Pigment-laden macrophages are not an expected finding.

Whipple's disease
Whipple's disease is incorrect. This can cause diarrhoea and weight loss. You might also expect the patient to have joint pains, hyper-pigmented skin and lymphadenopathy, which are not mentioned in this case. The diagnosis is made endoscopically by finding PAS-positive macrophages in the lamina propria containing nonacid-fast, Gram-positive bacilli indicating Tropheryma whipplei. This can be done by culture or polymerase chain reaction. We are told no organisms were identified and so this is not the correct diagnosis.

stem: A 17-year-old male is admitted to the neurology ward with a 2-month history of tremor, difficulty with speech and changes in behaviour. On examination, he has mild hepatomegaly and a greenish-brown ring at the corneal margin. His laboratory results are as follows: Serum caeruloplasmin 0.09 g/L (0.20–0.40) ALT 88 IU/L (5–35) Bilirubin 36 µmol/L (3–21) What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
Penicillamine
Penicillamine is the correct answer because it is the traditional first-line chelating agent for Wilson’s disease according to UK guidelines. It binds copper, increasing urinary excretion and reducing tissue deposition. The scenario describes a young patient with hepatic and neurological features, low caeruloplasmin, and Kayser-Fleischer rings—classic for Wilson’s disease. Early initiation of penicillamine can prevent progression and improve symptoms.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect as corticosteroids are not used in the management of Wilson’s disease unless there is concomitant autoimmune hepatitis or fulminant hepatic failure requiring immunosuppression, which this patient does not have.

Azathioprine
Azathioprine is an immunosuppressant used mainly in autoimmune conditions such as autoimmune hepatitis or inflammatory bowel disease but has no role in treating Wilson's disease where copper chelation is required.

Lactulose
Lactulose may be used to treat hepatic encephalopathy by reducing ammonia absorption from the gut but does not address copper overload or its consequences; it would not be first-line therapy here.

Trientine
Trientine, while also an effective chelator for copper, is currently reserved for patients intolerant of penicillamine or who develop side effects from it; it may become first-line in future but current UK practice recommends penicillamine initially.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a progressive history of fatigue, joint, and abdominal pain, and a bronze, greying of his skin. Base-level blood tests are shown below. Albumin 20 g/L 35-55 ALT 68 U/L 10-40 Alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L 25-100 INR 1.9 >1.1 HbA1c 8% 4-5.6 An element absorption and metabolism disorder is suspected and genetic testing confirms the presence of a specific mutation causing the condition. Venesection is started as a first-line treatment. What measurement is used along with ferritin to monitor this patient's treatment?
explanation:
Transferrin saturation
Ferritin and transferrin saturation are used to monitor treatment in haemochromatosis. This patient has presented with the autosomal recessive iron absorption and metabolism disorder haemochromatosis. Patients normally develop complications of the condition after the age of 40 with common features including liver failure, type 2 diabetes, arthritis, and a bronze, greying of the skin. Diagnosis can be confirmed by identifying raised ferritin and transferrin saturation levels or via molecular genetic testing for the C282Y and H63D mutations. Venesection is the first-line treatment for the condition which is monitored via ferritin and transferrin saturation testing with target levels below 50ug/l and 50% respectively.

Desferrioxamine
Desferrioxamine is an iron chelator that can be used as an alternative treatment for haemochromatosis if venesection cannot be performed. It acts by binding to free iron in the bloodstream and increasing elimination in the urine. Desferrioxamine is a medication and is, therefore, a separate form of treatment from venesection.

Haemoglobin
Haemoglobin (Hb) is an iron-containing protein found in red blood cells and, although reduced in iron deficits, a patient's Hb level is relatively unaffected in iron overload. For this reason, it should not be measured to monitor venesection treatment of haemochromatosis.

Serum iron
Serum iron is a measurement of the total amount of circulating iron bound to both transferrin and ferritin. This level can be affected by several other factors such as haemoglobin levels and therefore the measurement has no value when attempting to diagnose haemochromatosis. It is the storage and excess of iron that is crucial to confirm the diagnosis and this is performed via ferritin and transferrin saturation.

Total iron-binding capacity
Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) is a specific investigation that measures a patient's blood capacity to bind iron to transferrin. Although mainly used for establishing the cause of anaemia, TIBC levels are normally low in haemochromatosis which can assist in confirming the diagnosis. Again TIBC levels are not commonly used to monitor venesection treatment.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with fatigue and intermittent episodes of diarrhoea for many years. She also experiences bloating and has lost 4kg in weight. Her examination is unremarkable and blood tests reveal the following: Hb 104 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 254 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.5 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) MCV 72 fL (80-100) Ferritin 3 ng/mL (10 to 120) Given the most likely diagnosis, tissue transglutaminase antibodies are also checked, which come back positive. Additionally, which of the following total serum levels should be checked?
explanation:
IgA
You cannot interpret TTG level in coeliac disease without looking at the IgA level. The correct answer is the IgA level. The likely diagnosis here, given the history and iron deficiency anaemia, is coeliac disease. Serology for this usually involves tissue transglutaminase (TTG-IgA) antibodies and endomysial antibodies (also IgA). There is, however, an association between coeliac disease and selective IgA deficiency - in patients with the latter condition, false-negative coeliac results may therefore be obtained. As such, it is important to check the total serum IgA level, to put the TTG-IgA and endomysial IgA levels into context.

IgD
The other classes are therefore incorrect as these do not relate to normal coeliac serology.

IgE
The other classes are therefore incorrect as these do not relate to normal coeliac serology.

IgG
The other classes are therefore incorrect as these do not relate to normal coeliac serology.

IgM
The other classes are therefore incorrect as these do not relate to normal coeliac serology.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain that is associated with alternating diarrhoea and constipation. Which one of the following symptoms is least consistent with a diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome?
options: Waking at night due to the pain
explanation:
Waking at night due to the pain
Pain which wakes a patient at night is not a feature that would be expected in irritable bowel syndrome.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presented with difficulty swallowing, chronic cough associated with occasional swellings in the neck. She had a recent admission where she was treated with intravenous antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia. She was reviewed on this occasion by the gastroenterology team who were concerned about her symptoms and feel she is at risk of further aspiration. They decided to perform an urgent barium swallow investigation. What is the barium swallow most likely to show?
explanation:
Pharyngeal pouch
Dysphagia, aspiration pneumonia, halitosis → ?pharyngeal pouch Pharyngeal pouch: In an older patient with dysphagia, chronic cough, intermittent neck swellings and a recent aspiration pneumonia, the picture is classic for a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker’s diverticulum). Barium swallow typically shows a posterior midline outpouching arising just above the cricopharyngeus at Killian’s dehiscence; contrast pools in the sac with possible overflow/aspiration. It uniquely explains the palpable/gurgling neck swelling and regurgitation of undigested food that trigger cough and aspiration, so this is the best fit.

Achalasia
Achalasia: Achalasia causes progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids from onset with nocturnal regurgitation and weight loss, but not intermittent neck swellings. On barium swallow you’d expect a dilated, aperistaltic oesophagus with “bird’s-beak” tapering at the lower oesophageal sphincter—findings centred distally, not at the hypopharynx. While aspiration can occur in achalasia, it does not account for a neck lump that fills/empties with swallowing, making this option inconsistent with the case.

Barrett's oesophagus
Barrett’s oesophagus: Barrett’s is a histological diagnosis (intestinal metaplasia due to chronic GORD) and is not identified by a barium swallow. Patients usually report long-standing heartburn and reflux rather than cough from pharyngeal regurgitation or a fluctuating neck mass. A barium study would not “show Barrett’s”; endoscopy with biopsies is required, and Barrett’s does not explain the aspiration pneumonia via pharyngeal stasis, so this is not the correct answer.

Diffuse oesophageal spasm
Diffuse oesophageal spasm: DES presents with intermittent chest pain and dysphagia often precipitated by hot/cold liquids; the barium swallow shows a “corkscrew”/“rosary bead” mid-oesophageal appearance due to simultaneous non-propagated contractions. It does not produce a lateral neck swelling or a reservoir of retained food in the hypopharynx, and aspiration pneumonia is less typical. The anatomical level and symptom pattern therefore do not match.

Oesophageal stricture
Oesophageal stricture: Benign peptic strictures cause slowly progressive dysphagia to solids (then liquids) with reflux history; barium swallow shows a smooth tapered narrowing (“rat-tail”) usually in the distal oesophagus. This does not account for episodic neck swellings or gurgling/regurgitation of undigested food into the mouth, and aspiration from proximal stasis is less characteristic. The localisation and clinical features make stricture unlikely here.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset abdominal pain and nausea. She has no past medical history and takes the combined oral contraceptive pill regularly. On examination, her observations are normal. Her abdomen is distended with tenderness in the right upper quadrant and a palpable liver edge. Shifting dullness is present. Investigations: Hb 123 g/L (115 - 160) Platelets 299 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 9.3 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Creatinine 90 µmol/L (55 - 120) Bilirubin 30 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 150 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 248 u/L (3 - 40) Albumin 30 g/L (35 - 50) What is the next most appropriate investigation to order?
explanation:
Doppler ultrasound liver
Budd-Chiari syndrome - ultrasound with Doppler flow studies is very sensitive and should be the initial radiological investigation. This woman has a diagnosis of Budd-Chiari syndrome. Budd-Chiari syndrome or hepatic vein thrombosis is more commonly associated with a hypercoagulable state (e.g. pregnancy, combined oral contraceptive pill use, malignancy and polycythaemia). Liver function tests tend to show a markedly raised ALT. Jaundice may be present but not always in the acute presentation. The investigation of choice is a doppler ultrasound of the liver to show the hepatic vein thrombus.

Alpha-fetoprotein
Alpha-fetoprotein is a tumour marker used to aid the detection of malignancies such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). HCC presents late with features of liver cirrhosis including jaundice, ascites and right upper quadrant pain. Typically in patients with cirrhosis, liver enzymes remain relatively normal with the most prominent derangements being a raised INR, reduced blood sugar and reduced albumin levels.

Ascitic tap
An ascitic tap can be a useful investigation to determine the aetiology of the underlying condition and to rule out infectious causes such as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. However, the lack of a significant inflammatory response makes infection less likely. Furthermore, an ascitic tap is not the investigation of choice in Budd-Chiari syndrome.

Computed tomography (CT) abdomen
A CT abdomen can show signs of Budd-Chiari syndrome such as enhancement of the caudate lobe and central liver around the inferior vena cava but is not used in the first instance.

Liver biopsy
A liver biopsy is associated with multiple complications including infection and bleeding. It is less frequently used in the diagnosis of hepatic disorders and plays no role in the investigation of Budd-Chiari syndrome.

stem: A known alcoholic presents to the emergency department with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and a serum amylase of 1653U/L. According to either the Glasgow or Ranson scoring systems, which of the following indicate severe pancreatitis?
options: Serum amylase five times the upper limit of normal
explanation:
Hypocalcaemia
Hypocalcaemia is an indicator of pancreatitis severity. Hypocalcaemia occurs in pancreatitis due to the saponification of fats. As lipase leaks out of the damaged pancreas, it breaks down fat into triglycerides and fatty acids. Fatty acids combine with calcium to produce soap. Therefore, reduced serum calcium can be used as a surrogate marker for the level of enzymatic damage in pancreatitis.

Hypercalcaemia
Whilst hypercalcaemia can cause pancreatitis, it is not an indicator of severe pancreatitis according to the Glasgow or Ranson scoring systems.

Serum amylase five times the upper limit of normal
Raised serum amylase is useful in the diagnosis of pancreatitis but does not feature in the Glasgow or Ranson scores for severity.

Raised serum lipase
Raised serum lipase is useful in the diagnosis of pancreatitis but does not feature in the Glasgow or Ranson scores for severity.

Raised C-reactive protein
Raised C-reactive protein is useful in the diagnosis of inflammation but does not feature in the Glasgow or Ranson scores for severity.

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to the acute medical unit with sudden-onset severe upper abdominal pain and marked abdominal distension. She reports no previous liver disease but has recently noticed her legs swelling. Examination reveals tender hepatomegaly and ascites. Laboratory investigations show: ALT 132 IU/L (5–40) Albumin 28 g/L (35–50) Bilirubin 54 µmol/L (3–17) Platelets 410 * 109/L (150–400) She is not pregnant and does not take any regular medication. What is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Antithrombin III deficiency
Budd-Chiari syndrome is most likely due to a thrombophilia. Antithrombin III deficiency is the correct answer because Budd-Chiari syndrome, or hepatic vein thrombosis, most commonly arises due to an underlying prothrombotic state such as a hereditary thrombophilia. Antithrombin III deficiency is one of the classic inherited causes, along with protein C and S deficiencies and factor V Leiden mutation. The scenario describes acute hepatic venous outflow obstruction—sudden-onset abdominal pain, ascites, tender hepatomegaly—in a young woman without risk factors for cirrhosis or chronic liver disease, making a procoagulant disorder most likely according to UK guidelines.

Autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis typically presents with insidious onset of symptoms such as fatigue, jaundice, or mild transaminitis rather than acute vascular obstruction features. While it can cause chronic liver dysfunction and cirrhosis over time, it would not directly lead to sudden hepatic vein thrombosis or Budd-Chiari syndrome in the absence of other thrombotic risk factors.

Alcoholic liver disease
Alcoholic liver disease generally results from prolonged heavy alcohol consumption leading to steatosis, alcoholic hepatitis, or cirrhosis. It rarely manifests acutely with severe pain and ascites unless advanced decompensated cirrhosis develops. There are no features in this scenario suggesting a history of alcohol misuse or stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease, an inherited copper metabolism disorder, usually presents in younger patients with neuropsychiatric signs or chronic liver dysfunction rather than acute hepatic vein thrombosis. The laboratory findings here do not suggest haemolysis or low ceruloplasmin; nor are there neurological symptoms described.

Viral hepatitis B infection
Viral hepatitis B infection may cause acute hepatitis but does not typically present with isolated hepatic vein thrombosis unless complicated by fulminant hepatic failure—which would be accompanied by coagulopathy and encephalopathy. There is also no mention of risk factors for viral transmission or prodromal illness.

stem: A 39-year-old man is admitted to hospital with decompensated liver disease of unknown aetiology. As part of a liver screen the following results are obtained: Anti-HBs Positive Anti-HBc Negative HBs antigen Negative Anti-HBs = Hepatitis B Surface Antibody; Anti-HBc = Hepatitis B Core Antibody; HBs antigen = Hepatitis B Surface Antigen What is this man's hepatitis B status?
explanation:
Previous immunisation to hepatitis B
The presence of positive Anti-HBs (Hepatitis B Surface Antibody) and negative Anti-HBc (Hepatitis B Core Antibody) and HBs antigen (Hepatitis B Surface Antigen) indicates that the patient has been previously immunised against hepatitis B. This is because the presence of Anti-HBs shows that the immune system has mounted a response against the virus, but the absence of Anti-HBc and HBs antigen suggests that there is no active infection or exposure to the virus.

Chronic hepatitis B - highly infectious
Chronic hepatitis B - highly infectious is incorrect because this would be indicated by a positive HBs antigen, which signifies an ongoing infection with hepatitis B. Additionally, in chronic infections, both AntiHBs and Anti-HBc are usually positive.

Probable hepatitis D infection
Probable hepatitis D infection is incorrect because hepatitis D infection occurs as a co-infection or superinfection with hepatitis B. Therefore, if there was a probable hepatitis D infection, we would expect to see evidence of active hepatitis B infection such as a positive HBs antigen.

Acute hepatitis B infection
Acute hepatitis B infection is incorrect because during an acute infection, both HBs antigen and Anti-HBc would typically be positive. In this case, both are negative, indicating no current or past exposure to the virus.

Chronic hepatitis B - not infectious
Chronic hepatitis B - not infectious is incorrect because this status would be characterized by a positive Anti-HBs along with positive AntiHBc and negative HBs antigen. This indicates that although there was prior exposure to the virus leading to immunity development (positive Anti-HBs), there is no ongoing active infection (negative HBs antigen). However, in this patient's case, both HBs antigen and Anti-HBc are negative, pointing towards previous immunisation rather than past infection.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has 8 months of progressive fatigue, pruritus, and mild right upper quadrant discomfort. Her history includes Sjogren's syndrome, and she has never drunk alcohol or smoked. She has mild scleral icterus, hepatomegaly, and skin excoriations. Her abdomen is otherwise non-distended and soft. Investigations: Bilirubin 35 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 280 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 73 u/L (3 - 40) IgM 4.5 g/L (0.4 - 2.5) Anti-nuclear antibodies positive Anti-mitochondrial antibodies positive Which further test must be performed before a definitive diagnosis can be made?
explanation:
Abdominal ultrasound
Imaging is required before making a diagnosis of PBC to exclude extrahepatic biliary obstruction. Abdominal ultrasound is correct. This 52-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pruritus, scleral icterus, hepatomegaly, and a cholestatic liver profile (raised ALP and mildly raised ALT), all of which point toward primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). Her positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies, raised IgM, and history of Sjögren’s syndrome further support this diagnosis. However, before confirming PBC, it is essential to exclude extrahepatic causes of cholestasis such as gallstones, strictures, or malignancy. Abdominal ultrasound is the first-line investigation to evaluate the biliary tree and liver parenchyma because it is non-invasive, accessible, and effective in identifying biliary dilatation or obstructive pathology. If no obstruction is seen and suspicion for PBC remains, more specific imaging such as MRCP may follow.

CT abdomen with contrast
CT abdomen with contrast is incorrect because it is not the first-line test for suspected PBC. Although it can detect large lesions or masses causing biliary obstruction, it involves unnecessary radiation and is less sensitive than ultrasound or MRCP for detecting small duct abnormalities. In this patient with no signs of malignancy (e.g. weight loss or palpable mass), and a likely autoimmune cause given the AMA positivity and Sjögren’s history, an ultrasound is more appropriate. CT may be considered if imaging later suggests malignancy or if symptoms suggest an alternative cause, such as pancreatic or biliary cancer.

Gallbladder biopsy
Gallbladder biopsy is incorrect as it is not relevant to the diagnosis of PBC, which affects the intrahepatic bile ducts rather than the gallbladder. This invasive procedure is not part of routine workup and would not provide useful diagnostic information for PBC. It may be considered if imaging suggests gallbladder cancer or mass lesions causing biliary obstruction, which is not indicated in this case. Her symptoms and antibody profile instead point to an autoimmune cholestatic disease rather than gallbladder pathology.

Liver elastography (FibroScan)
Liver elastography (FibroScan) is incorrect as it assesses the degree of liver fibrosis, not the cause of cholestasis. While useful in monitoring known liver diseases, it is not helpful in excluding extrahepatic obstruction, which must be ruled out before confirming PBC. Additionally, cholestasis can falsely elevate stiffness readings, making it unreliable during active disease. In this patient, who has not yet had biliary imaging, liver elastography is premature and not part of the initial diagnostic pathway.

Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography
Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography is incorrect as it is an invasive imaging test used for therapeutic or highly detailed diagnostic purposes when ultrasound and MRCP are inconclusive. It carries procedural risks such as bleeding or infection and is not indicated without prior imaging. In this patient with suspected PBC, non-invasive imaging such as ultrasound is preferred first. PTC may only be appropriate if there is confirmed or suspected obstruction not well visualised by other methods, or in cases requiring intervention, such as biliary drainage.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). She occasionally experiences spasms of pain in the left iliac fossa and has periods of both constipation and loose stools. You are considering drug therapy to provide her with symptomatic relief from the symptoms. Which one of the following does NICE recommend that we avoid in patients with IBS?
explanation:
Lactulose
NICE recommend avoiding lactulose in the management of IBS. According to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, lactulose should be avoided in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) as it can exacerbate symptoms. Lactulose is a synthetic disaccharide that works by drawing water into the bowel, softening stools and increasing bowel movements. However, it can also cause bloating, flatulence, and abdominal discomfort, which are common symptoms of IBS.

Mebeverine
Mebeverine is an antispasmodic medication that helps relieve muscle spasms in the gastrointestinal tract. It is commonly prescribed for IBS patients to alleviate abdominal pain and cramping associated with the condition. Therefore, mebeverine would not be contraindicated for use in IBS patients.

Ispaghula
Ispaghula, also known as psyllium husk, is a bulk-forming laxative derived from the seeds of the Plantago ovata plant. It works by absorbing water in the intestines, forming a gel-like substance that promotes softer stool consistency and easier passage through the colon. Ispaghula may help improve both constipation and diarrhea symptoms in IBS patients.

Methylcellulose
Methylcellulose is another bulk-forming laxative similar to ispaghula. It absorbs water in the intestines and increases stool bulk, making it easier for stools to pass through the colon. Methylcellulose may help manage constipation-related symptoms of IBS without causing significant side effects or worsening other IBS symptoms.

Sterculia
Finally, Sterculia is a natural gum extracted from the Sterculia species of trees. It acts as a bulk-forming laxative by absorbing water and increasing fecal mass while softening stools. Sterculia can be used to manage constipation in IBS patients and is generally well-tolerated.

stem: You are the medical doctor on call. A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of loose stools, abdominal pain and fatigue. She tells you that she has been opening her bowels on average 7 times a day, and that in the last 24 hours she has noticed blood mixed in with the stools. The patient has a past medical history of ulcerative colitis, which is usually well controlled with rectal mesalazine. She has no other medical history and no allergies. On examination, the blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg, heart rate 95 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 96% and temperature 37.9 ºC. Heart sounds are normal, chest is clear. Abdomen is soft, with localised tenderness in the left iliac fossa. There is no guarding or peritonism and bowel sounds are heard. Hb 102 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 398 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 13.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na 140 mmol/L (135 - 145) K 3.8 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 4.6 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 95 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 35 mg/L (< 5) You suspect a flare of ulcerative colitis. How should this patient be managed?
explanation:
Admit + IV hydrocortisone
A severe flare of ulcerative colitis should be treated in hospital with IV corticosteroids. This patient has a severe flare, as she is opening her bowels >6 times per day with blood, she is tachycardic (HR >90) and febrile (temperature >37.5ºC). She is also anaemic (Hb <105) with raised inflammatory markers (CRP >30). Treatment of acute severe ulcerative colitis can be life-threatening, and requires immediate hospital admission. All patients should be treated with IV corticosteroids (hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone) in order to induce remission.

Admit + IV ciclosporin
If intravenous corticosteroids are contra-indicated, declined or cannot be tolerated, then intravenous ciclosporin may be considered as 2nd line.

Admit + PO prednisolone
For patients who have no improvement within 72 hours of starting IV corticosteroids or whose symptoms worsen despite treatment, consider adding ciclosporin and consider surgical management.

Admit + IV infliximab
Infliximab may be used to treat acute severe ulcerative colitis if ciclosporin is contraindicated.

stem: A 44-year-old man with alcoholic liver disease is admitted with pyrexia. He has been unwell for the past three days and has multiple previous admissions before with variceal bleeding. Examination shows multiple stigmata of chronic liver disease, ascites and jaundice. Paracentesis is performed with the following results: Neutrophils 487 cells/ul What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Intravenous cefotaxime
This patient has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), a common and potentially fatal infection in patients with cirrhotic ascites. The diagnosis of SBP is made when the neutrophil count in the ascitic fluid is greater than 250 cells/ul, as seen in this patient. According to UK guidelines, the first-line treatment for SBP is intravenous cefotaxime or a similar third-generation cephalosporin. These antibiotics cover most of the organisms commonly implicated in SBP, including Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and pneumococci.

Therapeutic abdominal washout
Therapeutic abdominal washout is not recommended for managing SBP. This procedure involves surgically opening the abdomen and washing out infected material, which can be highly invasive and carries significant risk. It's typically reserved for cases where there's an intraabdominal source of infection that needs to be removed, such as perforated bowel or abscesses - conditions not suggested by this scenario.

Intravenous vancomycin + metronidazole
Intravenous vancomycin + metronidazole could be considered if there was suspicion of infection with resistant Gram-positive bacteria or anaerobes, but these are not typically the causative organisms in SBP. Moreover, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy should generally be avoided unless absolutely necessary due to concerns about antibiotic resistance.

Insert an ascitic drain
The option Insert an ascitic drain would likely exacerbate rather than improve this patient's condition. Draining ascitic fluid can lead to hypovolaemia and renal failure in cirrhotic patients and doesn't treat the underlying infection causing SBP.

Intravenous ciprofloxacin
Intravenous ciprofloxacin could theoretically be used as it does have activity against some of the common causative organisms in SBP. However, cefotaxime or another third-generation cephalosporin would generally be preferred due to their broader spectrum of coverage and better efficacy demonstrated in clinical trials.

stem: A 55-year-old inpatient with decompensated liver cirrhosis experiences high fever and reduced urine output. Investigations are performed including paracentesis of the peritoneal fluid which revealed a neutrophil count of 310 cells/µL indicating spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Culture of the peritoneal fluid would most likely isolate which of the following organisms?
explanation:
Escherichia coli
The most common organism found on ascitic fluid culture is E. coli. The most common causative organisms of SBP are gram-negative enteric bacteria. E coli is by far the most common followed by Klebsiella.

Klebsiella pneumoniae
Klebsiella pneumoniae is a common causative organism of SBP, but it is less common than E. coli.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
The most common gram-positive organism causing SBP is Streptococcus pneumoniae, but it is less common than gram-negative organisms like E. coli.

Streptococcus viridans
Streptococcus viridans is a gram-positive organism that can cause SBP, but it is less common than E. coli.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is a gram-positive organism that can cause SBP, but it is less common than E. coli.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with a history of alcoholic liver disease is reviewed in clinic. She has advanced cirrhosis and has started to accumulate ascites. An ascitic tap was recently performed and showed a protein concentration of 12 g/L but no evidence of any organisms. What is the most appropriate management concerning the risk of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
explanation:
Oral ciprofloxacin
Patients with ascites (and protein concentration <= 15 g/L) should be given oral ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin as prophylaxis against spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. The correct answer in this case is Oral ciprofloxacin. In patients with advanced cirrhosis and low ascitic fluid protein (<15 g/L), there is an increased risk of developing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Oral ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that provides broad-spectrum coverage against Gram-negative organisms, which are the most common cause of SBP. According to UK guidelines, long-term prophylaxis with oral ciprofloxacin (or norfloxacin) should be considered for patients at high risk for SBP, such as those with a previous episode of SBP or low ascitic fluid protein concentration.

No antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated
No antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated would not be appropriate in this case due to the patient's increased risk for SBP based on her low ascitic fluid protein concentration and history of advanced cirrhosis.

Oral penicillin
Oral penicillin is not an appropriate choice for SBP prophylaxis because it does not provide adequate coverage against Gram-negative organisms commonly implicated in SBP, such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae.

Oral azithromycin
Oral azithromycin, a macrolide antibiotic, is also not suitable for SBP prophylaxis as it primarily targets Gram-positive bacteria and atypical organisms. It does not have sufficient activity against Gram-negative bacteria frequently associated with SBP.

Oral doxycycline
Oral doxycycline, a tetracycline antibiotic, provides broader coverage than penicillin but still lacks optimal effectiveness against the typical causative organisms of SBP. Moreover, doxycycline has potential hepatotoxic effects which could further worsen liver function in a patient with advanced cirrhosis.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding gastrin is true?
options: Secreted by D cells in the stomach
Secretion is inhibited by high antral pH
Reduces acid secretion in the stomach
Distension of the stomach inhibits secretion
explanation:
Increases gastric motility
Gastrin - increases gastric motility. Increases gastric motility is the correct answer. Gastrin is a peptide hormone primarily produced by G cells in the gastric antrum and duodenum. One of its key physiological actions is to increase gastric motility. Gastrin stimulates smooth muscle contraction in the stomach, which enhances gastric mixing and emptying. This effect is part of gastrin's overall role in promoting digestion. By increasing gastric motility, gastrin helps to mix food with gastric secretions and facilitates the movement of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum.

Secreted by D cells in the stomach
Secreted by D cells in the stomach is incorrect. Gastrin is produced by G cells, not D cells, in the gastric antrum and duodenum. D cells in the gastrointestinal tract secrete somatostatin, which actually inhibits gastrin release and gastric acid secretion. This is an important regulatory mechanism in the stomach to prevent excessive acid production.

Secretion is inhibited by high antral pH
Secretion is inhibited by high antral pH is incorrect. The opposite is true - gastrin secretion is inhibited by low antral pH (acidic environment) and stimulated by high antral pH (alkaline environment). This represents a negative feedback mechanism whereby gastrin stimulates acid secretion, and when the pH becomes sufficiently acidic, gastrin secretion is inhibited. This prevents excessive acid production that could damage the gastric mucosa.

Reduces acid secretion in the stomach
Reduces acid secretion in the stomach is incorrect. Gastrin actually stimulates acid secretion in the stomach. It acts on the parietal cells of the gastric glands, either directly or by stimulating histamine release from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells, to increase hydrochloric acid production. This is one of the primary functions of gastrin in the digestive process.

Distension of the stomach inhibits secretion
Distension of the stomach inhibits secretion is incorrect. Gastric distension (stretching of the stomach wall) actually stimulates gastrin secretion rather than inhibiting it. This is part of the normal physiological response to food intake. When food enters the stomach causing distension, gastrin secretion increases to promote acid secretion and gastric motility, facilitating digestion.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with 4 episodes of non-bloody diarrhoea in a 24-hour period. He has a past medical history of ulcerative colitis. Observations are within normal limits. He is started on rectal aminosalicylates however there is no improvement. Blood results are as follows: Hb 145 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) WBC 8.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 138 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.4 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 6.2 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 74 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 8 mg/L (< 5) ESR 12 mm/hr Men: < (age / 2) Women: < ((age + 10) / 2) A colonoscopy is performed: Colonoscopy Diffuse superficial ulceration from the rectum to the hepatic flexure What treatment is indicated?
explanation:
Oral aminosalicylates
As the patient has a mild flare-up of ulcerative colitis with demonstrable disease extending past the left-sided colon, oral aminosalicylates are the agent of choice as enemas only reach the splenic flexure.

Intravenous ciclosporin
Intravenous ciclosporin may be used in severe colitis if steroids are contraindicated.

Intravenous steroids
Intravenous steroids are usually given first-line for severe colitis. Features of severe disease include >6 bowel movements per day with systemic upset, visible blood, pyrexia, tachycardia (>90 beats per minute), anaemia, and an ESR >30mm/hour.

Methotrexate
Research on the use of methotrexate for ulcerative colitis has shown that it is not generally effective and it is therefore not a recommended treatment.

Rectal mesalazine
As the patient has demonstrable disease extending past the left-sided colon, oral aminosalicylates are the agent of choice as enemas only reach so far.

stem: A 52-year-old originally presents with frequent, on-off epigastric discomfort and burning, radiating up to the throat, commonly associated with certain food types. A gastroscope reveals evidence of significant gastritis but H.pylori testing is inconclusive. He is commenced on omeprazole and two antibiotics which improved his symptoms but on completing the course his symptoms returned a few days later. As such he was recommenced on the omeprazole long term. What adverse effect is the patient at risk of?
explanation:
Clostridium difficile infections
Omeprazole can increase your risk of severe diarrhoea (Clostridium difficile infections) Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) commonly commenced to reduce gastric acid production in conditions such as gastritis. As a frequently prescribed drug, it is often thought of as having little to no adverse effects however several complications can arise from its use. The significant inhibitor of gastric acid production resulting from PPIs use can lead to the proliferation of Clostridium difficile spores, normally destroyed by the low pH. PPIs are also thought to impair gastric leukocyte function, inhibiting phagocytosis and therefore increasing the risk of Clostridium difficile establishment and infection.

Hypermagnesemia
Hypomagnesemia, and not hypermagnesemia, has been strongly associated with PPI use. Although the mechanism is not fully understood it is believed that PPI use results in a decrease of active magnesium (Mg2+) absorption from the intestines.

Hypernatremia
