explanation:
The correct answer is cholestyramine. This patient has had removal of
the main area of inflammation but has ongoing symptoms. There is no
evidence of ongoing inflammation biochemically. Clinically, diarrhoea
without blood or mucus is also less suggestive of inflammation. In
patients who have had the ileum removed, bile acid malabsorption is a
major cause of diarrhoea as most bile acids are reabsorbed in the ileum.
This condition can be treated with cholestyramine.
Corticosteroids is incorrect. This would be appropriate for a patient with
a recurrence of Crohn's colitis. However, this patient has no evidence of
inflammation biochemically or clinically so this would not be indicated at
this time.
Infliximab is incorrect. This is generally used for Crohn's colitis
refractory to first-line agents. As discussed, this patient does not appear
to have ongoing inflammation and bile acid malabsorption is a more
likely cause of the symptoms.
Metronidazole is incorrect. This antibiotic is used for some intestinal
infections such as giardiasis. In the context of Crohn's, it may be used
for complications such as abscess or peritonitis, usually in combination
with a gram-negative antibiotic. There is no evidence of infection or such
complications in the case described.
Referral for further surgery is incorrect. Surgery should be reserved for
patients with severe disease refractory to medical management. This
patient does not have evidence of inflammation. Even in the presence of
ongoing inflammation, further medical management would be indicated
before any further surgical intervention.
Ongoing diarrhoea in Crohn's patient post-resection with normal
CRP → cholestyramine
Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant used in the management of
hyperlipidaemia. It decreases bile acid reabsorption in the small
intestine, therefore upregulating the amount of cholesterol that is
converted to bile acid. The main effect it has on the lipid profile is to
reduce LDL cholesterol. It is also occasionally used in Crohn's disease
for treatment diarrhoea following bowel resection.
Adverse effects
abdominal cramps and constipation
decreases absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
cholesterol gallstones
may raise level of triglycerides

explanation:
This patient presents with Crohn's disease. The initial monotherapy of
prednisolone is effective at high dose but symptoms return on tapering
its dose. An add-on treatment is therefore needed. The next agent to
think about is azathioprine or mercaptopurine, in accordance with NICE
guidance. Before either is commenced, a TPMT level must be done. If it
is deficient, very low or absent, neither azathioprine or mercaptopurine
should be offered.
Methotrexate is the next most suitable agent to add if the patient cannot
tolerate mercaptopurine or azathioprine.
Infliximab is used only when patients have failed conventional therapy,
including immunosuppressives and corticosteroids.

correct initial management is with a combination of oral vancomycin and

Bezlotoxumab is incorrect. This is a human monoclonal antitoxin

practice and would not be used to treat the acute infection.

Clostridium difficile infection or as a second-line therapy in a first
infection but would be inadequate to treat a life-threatening infection.

presentation of Clostridium difficile infection that is not life threatening.
In life-threatening C. difficile infection treatment is with ORAL
vancomycin and IV metronidazole

megacolon (transverse colon diameter > 6cm) or ileus, which is
reassuring.
Clostridioides difficile
Clostridioides difficile is a Gram positive rod often encountered in
hospital practice. It produces an exotoxin which causes intestinal
damage leading to a syndrome called pseudomembranous colitis. C.
difficile develops when the normal gut flora are suppressed by broad-
spectrum antibiotics. Clindamycin is historically associated with causing
C. difficile but the aetiology has evolved significantly over the past 10
years. Second and third-generation cephalosporins are now the leading
cause of C. difficile.
Other than antibiotics, risk factors include:
proton pump inhibitors
Pathophysiology
anaerobic gram-positive, spore-forming, toxin-producing bacillus
transmission: via the faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores
releases two exotoxins (toxin A and toxin B) that act on intestinal
epithelial cells and inflammatory cells resulting in colitis
Features
diarrhoea
abdominal pain
a raised white blood cell count (WCC) is characteristic
if severe toxic megacolon may develop

The patient has presented with symptoms and signs consistent with
Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, nystagmus) and dry beriberi
(peripheral neuropathy). There is a clinical association between
Hyperemesis gravidarum and thiamine deficiency, particularly when it is
prolonged and normal dietary intake is compromised. This patient
should receive high-dose parenteral thiamine without delay.
Intravenous dextrose administered before correction of thiamine
deficiency may exacerbate her condition and should be avoided.
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord would be one of the major
differentials in this case. However, the downgoing plantar responses and
presence of ocular signs make this less likely.
Niacin is used to treat pellagra. This patient is confused, but there is no
mention of diarrhoea or a skin rash in the vignette.
Vitamin B1 (thiamine)
Thiamine is a water soluble vitamin of the B complex group. One of it's
phosphate derivates, thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), is a coenzyme in
the following enzymatic reactions:
pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
pyruvate decarboxylase in ethanol fermentation
alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
branched-chain amino acid dehydrogenase complex
2-hydroxyphytanoyl-CoA lyase

explanation:
Hydrogen breath testing is an appropriate first line test for
diagnosis of small bowel overgrowth syndrome
When there is an increase in the bacterial colonization of the small
bowel proximal to the distal ileum, it is referred to as small bowel
bacterial overgrowth (SBBO). Patients can present with symptoms which
include weight loss, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and malnutrition. They
may also exhibit neurological symptoms associated with vitamin B12
malabsorption and impaired absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E,
and K). Hydrogen breath testing is a more commonly used first-line
investigation for making diagnosis of small bowel bacterial overgrowth
syndrome. Treatment of SBBO includes surgical correction of the
underlying abnormality, antibiotics (metronidazole is commonly used),
and treatment of dysmotility.
The other options'faecal calprotectin, flexible sigmoidoscopy, and
SeHCAT scan'may be useful to exclude other diagnoses, such as
inflammatory bowel disease, microscopic colitis, and bile acid
malabsorption, respectively. The faecal elastase test is used along with
other tests, such as fecal fat and/or fecal chymotrypsin, to evaluate both
children and adults for pancreatic insufficiency.
Small bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome
Small bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome (SBBOS) is a disorder
characterised by excessive amounts of bacteria in the small bowel
resulting in gastrointestinal symptoms.

This patient has multiple risk factors for a severe phenotype of Crohn's

severe phenotype, a rapid step-up to biological therapy is indicated.

terminal ill disease, although anastomotic recurrence remains common.

would not be sufficient to induce remission in this patient.

Hepatitis B DNA level is the correct answer. The patient has chronic
hepatitis B. The viral load i.e. hepatitis B DNA level is positive and
suggests ongoing viral activity. The viral load is the best marker in
determining the risk of developing cirrhosis.
ALT is incorrect. This is a marker of liver inflammation but is inferior to
the HBV DNA level in determining the risk of cirrhosis.
Hepatitis B core antibody is incorrect. This suggests that the patient has
caught hepatitis B at some point in time. It is not used to quantify the
risk of developing cirrhosis.
Hepatitis B e antigen is incorrect. This is a marker of infectivity and
correlates with HBV DNA levels but is less accurate in predicting the risk
of cirrhosis than HBV DNA levels.
Hepatitis B surface antigen is incorrect. HBsAg being positive implies
ongoing infection, either acute or chronic (if present > 6 months). It is
less accurate than HBV DNA in predicting those who will develop
cirrhosis.
Hepatitis B DNA levels are the best marker for determining the risk
of developing cirrhosis

Question 11 of 267
A 33-year-old lady has a diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). She
has previously been seen in the gastroenterology clinic and all
investigations including colonoscopy were normal. She is mainly
troubled by abdominal pain, bloating and constipation. She continues to
have symptoms despite the use of antispasmodics, regular Movicol
(macrogol laxative) and input from a dietician. She has tried other
laxatives in the past with limited benefit. What would be the next most
appropriate option?
explanation:
NICE have written guidance on the diagnosis and management of IBS.
First line pharmacological treatments include antispasmodics e.g.
hyoscine or mebeverine; loperamide for diarrhoea and laxatives for
constipation. Lactulose should be avoided.
2nd line options include tricyclic antidepressants e.g. up to 30mg
amitriptyline if above treatments have not helped
3rd line: serotonin selective reuptake inhibitors
Linaclotide can be considered if there has been no benefit from
different laxatives and the patient has had constipation for at least
12 months.
Other management options include dietary advice and psychological
treatments.
Acupuncture and reflexology are not recommended for managing IBS.

except a 'cough and cold' treated by his GP with 3 days of oral
augmentin last week. His past medical history includes hypertension,
gastric reflux and type 2 diabetes mellitus, for which he takes metformin,
ramipril and lansoprazole. On examination, abdomen generally tender
and distended, resonant to percussion. Bowel sounds are absent. Stool
cultures were initially sent three days ago but the results are still
awaited, the laboratory reports that the sample has been lost. A flexible
sigmoidoscopy was performed, with the report stating yellow
membranes in an inflamed sigmoid colon. What is the most likely
diagnosis?
options: Bacillus cereus infection from undercooked barbecue meats
explanation:
Fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea in the context of recent antibiotic use
and lansoprazole should raise suspicion for Clostridium difficile
infection. The colonoscopic description of yellow membranes is
suggestive of pseudomembranous colitis as a result of exudates and
cell debris from C diff infection. Bacillus cereus usually occurs within 24
hours, E Coli within 72 hours (with bloody stool) and giardiasis within 3
weeks. Diverticulitis would be seen on flexible sigmoidoscopy.
Clostridioides difficile
Clostridioides difficile is a Gram positive rod often encountered in
hospital practice. It produces an exotoxin which causes intestinal
damage leading to a syndrome called pseudomembranous colitis. C.
difficile develops when the normal gut flora are suppressed by broad-
spectrum antibiotics. Clindamycin is historically associated with causing
C. difficile but the aetiology has evolved significantly over the past 10
years. Second and third-generation cephalosporins are now the leading
cause of C. difficile.
Other than antibiotics, risk factors include:
proton pump inhibitors
Pathophysiology
anaerobic gram-positive, spore-forming, toxin-producing bacillus
transmission: via the faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores
releases two exotoxins (toxin A and toxin B) that act on intestinal
epithelial cells and inflammatory cells resulting in colitis
Features
diarrhoea
abdominal pain
a raised white blood cell count (WCC) is characteristic
if severe toxic megacolon may develop

determine treatment:

appearance of his skin and a significantly raised ferritin and MCV
without another obvious cause. The likely diagnosis is
haemochromatosis. These patients are at risk of developing

Macrophage activation syndrome is incorrect. This is a complication of
systemic autoimmune disease, most commonly, Adult-onset Still's
disease (AOSD), which is characterized by hyperferritinemia. However,
these patients tend to be systemically unwell with high fevers and

causes anaemia and a low MCV making the diagnosis unlikely in this

levels and this is a complication of excess alcohol use. However, this
patient drinks within recommended guidelines, making this diagnosis
unlikely.

this is a complication of excess alcohol use. However, this patient drinks
within recommended guidelines, making this diagnosis unlikely.

Hepatocellular carcinoma
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the third most common cause of
cancer worldwide. Chronic hepatitis B is the most common cause of
HCC worldwide with chronic hepatitis C being the most common cause
in Europe.
The main risk factor for developing HCC is liver cirrhosis, for example
secondary* to hepatitis B & C, alcohol, haemochromatosis and primary
biliary cirrhosis. Other risk factors include:
alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
hereditary tyrosinosis
glycogen storage disease
aflatoxin
drugs: oral contraceptive pill, anabolic steroids
porphyria cutanea tarda
male sex
diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome

tends to present late

RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, pruritus, splenomegaly
possible presentation is decompensation in a patient with chronic
liver disease
raised AFP

for high risk groups such as:
patients liver cirrhosis secondary to hepatitis B & C or
haemochromatosis
men with liver cirrhosis secondary to alcohol

presentation. It may be caused by a wide variety of conditions but is

explanation:
The most likely diagnosis in this case is primary biliary cirrhosis, as
evidenced by the patients severe tiredness, itching and positive
autoantibodies. The ratio of male:female is around 1:9, however it is
important to remember this disease does affect men as well.
Treatments are aimed at alleviation of symptoms and at slowing the
disease, although liver transplant can offer a cure. Ursodeoxycholic acid
has been shown to slow progression of the disease and improve the
symptoms of jaundice.
Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis (previously referred to as primary biliary
cirrhosis) is a chronic liver disorder typically seen in middle-aged
females (female:male ratio of 9:1). The aetiology is not fully understood
although it is thought to be an autoimmune condition. Interlobular bile
ducts become damaged by a chronic inflammatory process causing
progressive cholestasis which may eventually progress to cirrhosis. The
classic presentation is itching in a middle-aged woman
Associations
Sjogren's syndrome (seen in up to 80% of patients)
rheumatoid arthritis
systemic sclerosis
thyroid disease
Clinical features
early: may be asymptomatic (e.g. raised ALP on routine LFTs) or
fatigue, pruritus
cholestatic jaundice
hyperpigmentation, especially over pressure points
around 10% of patients have right upper quadrant pain
xanthelasmas, xanthomata
also: clubbing, hepatosplenomegaly
late: may progress to liver failure

explanation:
The management of hyponatraemia in liver cirrhosis is a difficult area
and a consensus hasn't been reached in all areas of management.
However in patients with mild hyponatraemia (126-135 mmol/L) the
recommendations are consistent. The British Society of
Gastroenterology recommendations are as follows:
Sodium 126-135 mmol/L with normal creatinine - Continue normal
diuretic regimen and observe, do not fluid restrict the patient.
Sodium 121-125 mmol/L with normal creatinine - International opinion is
to continue diuretics, however, the British Society of Gastroenterology
recommend a more cautious approach, and suggest either stopping
diuretics or reducing the dose.
Sodium 121-125 mmol/L with raised creatinine (>150 mmol/L or >120
mmol/L and rising) - Stop diuretics and volume expand with human
albumin solution 4.5%, gelofusine, or haemaccel
Sodium <121 mmol/L - Incredibly controversial, but the British society of
gastroenterology suggest stopping diuretics and volume expanding with
human albumin solution 4.5%, gelofusine, or haemaccel (which all
contain sodium concentrations similar to that of normal saline).
They do, however, recognise that the level of evidence for this
recommendation is 5 (or D) i.e. expert opinion, and further work needs to
be done into the role of volume expansion and fluid restriction in
cirrhosis.
Alcoholic liver disease
Alcoholic liver disease covers a spectrum of conditions:
alcoholic fatty liver disease
alcoholic hepatitis
cirrhosis
Selected investigation findings:
gamma-GT is characteristically elevated
the ratio of AST:ALT is normally > 2, a ratio of > 3 is strongly
suggestive of acute alcoholic hepatitis
Selected management notes for alcoholic hepatitis:
glucocorticoids (e.g. prednisolone) are often used during acute
episodes of alcoholic hepatitis
Maddrey's discriminant function (DF) is often used during acute
episodes to determine who would benefit from glucocorticoid
therapy
it is calculated by a formula using prothrombin time and
bilirubin concentration
pentoxyphylline is also sometimes used
the STOPAH study (see reference) compared the two common
treatments for alcoholic hepatitis, pentoxyphylline and
prednisolone. It showed that prednisolone improved survival at
28 days and that pentoxyphylline did not improve outcomes

explanation:
Obstetric cholestasis, also known as intrahepatic cholestasis of
pregnancy, is a condition caused by the impaired flow of bile. This, in
turn, causes a build up of bile salts which can then deposit in the skin
(causing pruritus) as well as the placenta. It is thought that the aetiology
of this condition is a combination of hormonal, genetic and
environmental factors.
Although the pruritic symptoms can be distressing for the mother, the
build up of bile salts can also be detrimental to foetal wellbeing. The
combination of the immature foetal liver's ability to cope with breaking
down the excessive bile salt levels as well as the vasoconstricting effect
of bile salts on human placental chorionic veins has been theorised to
be the cause of sudden asphyxial events in the foetus leading to anoxia
and death.
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (also known as obstetric
cholestasis) affects around 1% of pregnancies in the UK. It is associated
with an increased risk of premature birth.

be seeing things and her diarrhoea was becoming a problem again. She
also had an itchy rash predominantly on the back of her hands and

corticosteroids but this had made no improvement. On examination,
there was an erythematous, scaly rash on the dorsum of both hands and
around the neck, she had an abbreviated mental test score (AMTS) of
4/10 with no other positive findings.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pellagra is a rare condition in the United Kingdom but it is seen in
patients with carcinoid syndrome. It is caused by a deficiency in vitamin
B3, (Niacin) and classically presents as the '4 Ds' dermatitis, dementia,
diarrhoea and death. Niacin can be absorbed through the diet or
converted in vivo from tryptophan. Patients with carcinoid syndrome are
at increased risk as tryptophan stores are metabolised to serotonin.
Dermatomyositis characteristically presents with a heliotrope rash,
Gottron's papules and muscle weakness but does not cause confusion
or diarrhoea typically, carcinoid tumours rarely metastasise to the brain.
Beriberi is caused by thiamine deficiency and typically causes a
peripheral neuropathy, high-output cardiac failure and is associated with
weight loss.
Carcinoid tumours
Carcinoid syndrome
usually occurs when metastases are present in the liver and release
serotonin into the systemic circulation
may also occur with lung carcinoid as mediators are not 'cleared' by
the liver
Features
flushing (often the earliest symptom)
diarrhoea
bronchospasm
hypotension
right heart valvular stenosis (left heart can be affected in bronchial
carcinoid)
other molecules such as ACTH and GHRH may also be secreted
resulting in, for example, Cushing's syndrome
pellagra can rarely develop as dietary tryptophan is diverted to
serotonin by the tumour

Drug-induced liver disease
Drug-induced liver disease is generally divided into hepatocellular,
cholestatic or mixed. There is however considerable overlap, with some
drugs causing a range of changes to the liver
The following drugs tend to cause a hepatocellular picture:
paracetamol
sodium valproate, phenytoin
MAOIs
halothane
anti-tuberculosis: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide
statins
alcohol
amiodarone

antibiotics: flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav, erythromycin*

explanation:
The combination of neuropsychiatric features and deranged LFTs should
alert you to a possible diagnosis of Wilson's disease. Caeruloplasmin is
the most appropriate investigation as extremely low levels provide
strong evidence of Wilson's disease and are considered diagnostic if
associated with Keyser-Fleischer rings. 24-hour urinary copper is useful
in confirming the diagnosis but is more difficult to perform and would
not normally be requested first-line.
Serum ferritin and transferrin saturations are used to diagnose
haemochromatosis, whilst anti-LKM antibodies are found in autoimmune
hepatitis type 2. None of the final 3 options are likely to present in the
manner described above.
Wilson's disease
Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by
excessive copper deposition in the tissues. Metabolic abnormalities
include increased copper absorption from the small intestine and
decreased hepatic copper excretion. Wilson's disease is caused by a
defect in the ATP7B gene located on chromosome 13.
The onset of symptoms is usually between 10 - 25 years. Children
usually present with liver disease whereas the first sign of disease in
young adults is often neurological disease
Features result from excessive copper deposition in the tissues,
especially the brain, liver and cornea:
liver: hepatitis, cirrhosis

specific for diverticulitis.

explanation:
Prednisolone 40mg for 28 days has been shown to increase survival in
patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis. However, response to steroid
treatment should be re-evaluated at 7 days, as not all patients respond
and continuing immunosuppressive treatment in patients who are
unlikely to benefit may prove deleterious.
As a rule of thumb, an increase in bilirubin over the first 7-days indicates
non-response. The Lille score is a more formal method of assessment
that takes into account a range of demographic and laboratory values to
give a more nuanced evaluation. A Lille score of > 0.45 signifies the
failure of prednisolone and justifies its discontinuation. The 6-month
survival rate for this group of patients is approximately 25%, so
supportive treatment should be continued.
Switching non-responders to pentoxifylline has not been shown to be
beneficial.
The inflammatory cytokine TNF-α is thought to be key to the
pathophysiology of acute alcoholic hepatitis and several studies have
investigated the efficacy of anti-TNF-α therapies in this setting.
etanercept are associated with higher mortality rates at 2 and 6 months,
largely secondary to the development of acute infection. As a result,
these agents are not recommended for use in alcoholic hepatitis.
Alcoholic liver disease
Alcoholic liver disease covers a spectrum of conditions:
alcoholic fatty liver disease
alcoholic hepatitis
cirrhosis
Selected investigation findings:
gamma-GT is characteristically elevated
the ratio of AST:ALT is normally > 2, a ratio of > 3 is strongly
suggestive of acute alcoholic hepatitis
Selected management notes for alcoholic hepatitis:
glucocorticoids (e.g. prednisolone) are often used during acute
episodes of alcoholic hepatitis
Maddrey's discriminant function (DF) is often used during acute
episodes to determine who would benefit from glucocorticoid
therapy
it is calculated by a formula using prothrombin time and
bilirubin concentration
pentoxyphylline is also sometimes used
the STOPAH study (see reference) compared the two common
treatments for alcoholic hepatitis, pentoxyphylline and
prednisolone. It showed that prednisolone improved survival at
28 days and that pentoxyphylline did not improve outcomes

A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with
shortness of breath.
He reports several months of worsening diarrhoea and is now passing
over 10 watery motions per day.
On examination he is dyspnoeic at rest. The blood pressure is 104 /
77mmHg and the pulse rate is 90bpm and regular. Oxygen saturations
are 93% on room air. Chest auscultation reveals widespread mild
polyphonic wheeze and bibasal crackles. Jugular venous pressure is
elevated and C-V waves are present. There is a pansystolic murmur at
the left lower sternal border louder in inspiration. There is a palpable liver
edge 2cm below the costal margin.
Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Stool sample for ova, cysts and parasites
explanation:
A long history of diarrhoea along with signs consistent with tricuspid
regurgitation is suggestive of carcinoid syndrome. This is a a
paraneoplastic syndrome that is caused by endogenous secretion of
serotonin (chiefly) from carcinoid tumours.
About 50% of patients have cardiac abnormalities caused by serotonin-
induced fibrosis of the valvular endocardium, notably the tricuspid and
pulmonary valves. The majority of patients with cardiac involvement
present with signs of right heart failure secondary to severe dysfunction
of these right-sided valves.
The most useful initial test is the 24-hour urine levels of 5-HIAA (5-
hydroxyindoleacetic acid) - the end product of serotonin metabolism.
Growth hormone day curves are used to diagnose acromegaly.
24 hour urine VMA (Vanillylmandelic acid) is used in the investigation of
pheochromocytoma.
Stool culture could be used to exclude infective causes of diarrhoea but
will not confirm the diagnosis in this case.
Faecal calprotectin is a non-specific marker of gut inflammation and will
not confirm the diagnosis in this case.

explanation:
Autoimmune hepatitis is the correct answer. The patient presents with
unexplained fatigue, jaundice, and hepatomegaly, along with markedly
elevated transaminases (ALT and AST), suggesting hepatocellular injury.
Her anti-smooth muscle antibodies (1/60) are positive, and IgG (25 g/L)
is significantly elevated—both classic markers of autoimmune hepatitis.
Based on the significantly high serum ferritin, haemochromatosis may
be suspected. However, ferritin is an acute phase reactant and is
commonly elevated in autoimmune hepatitis due to inflammation.
Furthermore, elevated autoantibodies (anti-smooth muscle antibodies
and IgG) are not observed in hemochromatosis and should raise
suspicion for autoimmune hepatitis.
Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) often occurs in patients with
obesity (her BMI = 32), making it a consideration. However, it typically
shows a milder increase in transaminases. Autoantibody positivity and
raised IgG are not features of NASH, further ruling it out.
Primary biliary cholangitis is incorrect in this case. While it shares some
features of autoimmune hepatitis, such as fatigue and jaundice, ALP is
predominantly high, and transaminases (AST and ALT) are typically
normal. This contradicts the labs in this case, where transaminases are
significantly elevated and higher than ALP. The negative anti-
mitochondrial antibodies and normal IgM further exclude this possibility.
Deranged LFTs + anti-smooth muscle antibodies (SMA) → ?type 1
autoimmune hepatitis
primarily damaging mitochondria. Since AST is present in both the
cytosol and mitochondria, while ALT is mainly cytosolic, mitochondrial
injury leads to a higher release of AST and thus AST to ALT ratio (> 1).
Additionally, Wilson’s disease often causes low ALP due to impaired ALP
synthesis and bile flow. In this case, ALT is higher than AST, and ALP is
slightly raised, which does not match the typical pattern of Wilson’s
disease, making it unlikely.

endoscopy due to persistent symptoms of reflux.

junction. Biopsy taken.

negative.

Plan: Review in clinic with histology
The histology is back and reported as follows:
Squamous epithelium and squamocolumnar junctional mucosal with
reflux oesophagitis. Some goblet cells. Basal portions of the crypts
show nuclei limited to the basal half of cell cytoplasm without loss of

Question 31 of 267
A 64-year-old man comes to your clinic. He recently attended an
endoscopy due to persistent symptoms of reflux.
The gastroscopy report is as follows:
Oesophagus: 3cm pink mucosa arising from the gastroesophageal
junction. Biopsy taken.
Stomach: patchy antral erythema. Normal body and fundus. CLO
negative.
Duodenum: normal to second part.
Plan: Review in clinic with histology
The histology is back and reported as follows:
Squamous epithelium and squamocolumnar junctional mucosal with
reflux oesophagitis. Some goblet cells. Basal portions of the crypts
show nuclei limited to the basal half of cell cytoplasm without loss of
polarity in keeping with low-grade dysplasia.
Given the diagnosis, what is the preferred management option?
explanation:
Barrett's oesophagus: radiofrequency ablation is the preferred
treatment for low-grade dysplasia
The biopsy findings are in keeping with Barrett's oesophagus. The first
stage is metaplasia, where there is intestinal epithelium lining the lower
part of the oesophagus. The intestinal epithelium is made up of simple
columnar cells and goblet cells. In this case, this epithelium type is
found within the oesophagus and is indicative of intestinal metaplasia
here. The report also details features of dysplasia - cytological changes,
loss of polarity etc. You wouldn't be expected to know the specific
features of high-grade vs low-grade dysplasia for MRCP, and so the stem
clarifies that the findings are in keeping with low-grade dysplasia.
Radiofrequency ablation is the correct answer. This is the preferred
choice of treatment for Barrett's oesophagus with low-grade dysplasia.
Endoscopic mucosal resection is incorrect. Although this can be used as
a treatment option for Barrett's oesophagus with low-grade dysplasia, it
would not be the first-line option.
Oesophagectomy is incorrect. This treatment option may be appropriate
in cases of oesophageal cancer, however, there is no evidence of this on
the histology for this patient.
Regular low-dose omeprazole is incorrect. High dose proton-pump-
inhibitors can be used in the management of Barrett's oesophagus
where there is metaplasia, but low-dose omeprazole is not specifically
indicated.
Endoscopic surveillance is incorrect. This would be appropriate if the
histology had shown metaplasia only, however, in this case, as there is
evidence of dysplasia, it would not be the most appropriate option.
Barrett's oesophagus
Barrett's refers to the metaplasia of the lower oesophageal mucosa, with
the usual squamous epithelium being replaced by columnar epithelium.

explanation:

The most likely diagnosis in this patient is haemochromatosis, an

joint pain, impotence and fatigue. Late signs can include cirrhosis of the
liver and diabetes. A fasting transferrin saturation of greater than 55%
indicates iron accumulation and along with genotyping for the HFE gene,
this would be the most appropriate investigation to establish the
diagnosis of the disease.

The Emergency Medical Team were summoned by the urology team. A
62-year-old gentleman was admitted to the care of the urology team a
few hours ago complaining of haematuria and loin pain. A CT scan of his
abdomen revealed the presence of renal calculi and he was being
treated conservatively with intravenous saline hydration therapy, as well
as intravenous paracetamol 1g QDS and IV morphine 10mg stat boluses
when required. Approximately an hour ago he complained of distressing
nausea and vomiting and was administered metoclopramide 10mg IV
bolus with a good response. However, over the last few minutes he
developed severe neck stiffness and was unable to open his eyelids. His
jaw was locked and his tongue was protruding. He had a past medical
history comprising panic attacks, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension,
hypercholesterolaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 3 and
osteoarthritis. In addition to the above medication, his drug history
included diazepam 2mg TDS PRN, metformin 500mg TDS, gliclazide
80mg OD, ramipril 5mg OD, atorvastatin 20mg ON and naproxen 500mg
BD PRN.
Examination revealed the presence of an acutely compromised
gentleman. His head was rotated to the left and fixed in position, with a
protruding tongue and a fixed locked jaw. His eyelids were closed. His
back was arched, his upper limbs were flexed and his lower limbs were
extended. He was very distressed but was sustaining respiratory effort
with a respiratory rate of 32/min and oxygen saturations of 96% on air.
His chest was clear to auscultate and cardiovascular examination was
unremarkable except for the presence of a tachycardia of 132 bpm. His
blood pressure was 122/78 mmHg. His temperature was 37.4ºC. He
was unable to speak but seemed to be fully alert. His capillary blood
sugar was 8.2.
A 15 litre/min non-rebreathe oxygen mask was attached; he did not
tolerate a Guedel airway insertion. Intravenous access was secured.
What is the next single best immediate management step?
Crash bleep the anaesthetics team to assist in supporting his
airway
Administer IM lorazepam
Administer IV adrenaline
Administer IV dantrolene
Administer IM procyclidine

options: Crash bleep the anaesthetics team to assist in supporting his airway
explanation:
This gentleman suffered from an acute dystonic reaction secondary to
being administered a dopamine receptor antagonist, and this reaction
occurs not uncommonly with antipsychotic medications amongst other
medications. Prompt action is essential as untreated this condition may
lead to complete airway collapse. First line treatment in the UK is
procyclidine, a rapid acting anticholinergic, with benzodiazepines and
anticholinergic antihistamines 2nd and 3rd line respectively. One may
argue that option 1 is the most appropriate option, but in the above
situation his airway was intact (just!) and he was sustaining respiratory
effort. Anaesthetic input would assist with securing a compromised
airway, but would not address the cause of the compromise. Prompt
treatment may prevent further deterioration and therefore is the most
appropriate option here.
Metoclopramide
Metoclopramide is a D2 receptor antagonist* mainly used in the
management of nausea. Other uses include:
gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
prokinetic action is useful in gastroparesis secondary to diabetic
neuropathy

explanation:
Patient choice and involvement are particularly important in

prednisolone is the best option for her, you have to respect her decision
to decline.

contraindicated or cannot be tolerated, consider budesonide.
Budesonide is not as effective in inducing remission but does have

A 56-year-old gentleman presents to the emergency department with
worsening shortness of breath. He has a past medical history of
oesophageal cancer which was treated six months ago with an
oesophagectomy and postoperative chemotherapy and radiotherapy. He
has been in remission for three months. His shortness of breath has
progressed over one week and has been associated with distension of
his abdomen. On examination, there is dullness to percussion of both
lung bases with reduced air entry as well. His abdomen is tense with
shifting dullness, but not very tender. His skin is warm and well perfused.
His legs are not swollen and there is no tenderness or pitting oedema. A
chest X-ray demonstrates small bilateral pleural effusions. Which
treatment is most appropriate to relieve his shortness of breath?
options: Treatment dose low molecular weight heparin
explanation:
The correct answer is abdominal paracentesis. This is a patient with an
aggressive type of malignancy presenting with ascites and pleural
effusions. Both of these can cause shortness of breath as tense ascites
will make it difficult for the diaphragm to properly ventilate the lungs.
Since the ascites is tense and the pleural effusions are small
paracentesis is more likely to be helpful than a chest drain. The most
likely cause is malignant ascites and effusions as well. Low molecular
weight heparin is a treatment option for pulmonary embolism, but there
is little evidence for this as a cause.

explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is a paralytic ileus. The presence of flatus and
gas in the rectum suggests that there is not a complete mechanical
obstruction. The absent bowel sounds are also indicative of paralytic
ileus.
Paralytic ileus has many causes. Some of the commoner causes include
drugs, electrolyte abnormalities and post-surgery. The patient, in this
case, has hypokalaemia which should be corrected.
Prokinetic agents such as metoclopramide can be very effective in
incomplete bowel obstruction or paralytic ileus. However, they are
contraindicated in complete bowel obstruction and in the presence of
colic.
5HT3 antagonists (e.g ondansetron) and antimuscarinics (e.g. cyclizine
and hyoscine butylbromide) can slow down the gut, cause constipation,
and worsen an ileus.

Question 39 of 267
A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with
shortness of breath.
He reports several months of worsening diarrhoea and is now passing
over 10 watery motions per day.
On examination he is dyspnoeic at rest. The blood pressure is 104 /
77mmHg and the pulse rate is 90bpm and regular. Oxygen saturations
are 93% on room air. Chest auscultation reveals widespread mild
polyphonic wheeze and bibasal crackles. Jugular venous pressure is
elevated and C-V waves are present. There is a pansystolic murmur at
the left lower sternal border louder in inspiration. There is a palpable liver
edge 2cm below the costal margin.
Which is the most likely underlying heart valve pathology?
explanation:
A long history of diarrhoea along with signs consistent with tricuspid
regurgitation is suggestive of carcinoid syndrome. This is a a
paraneoplastic syndrome that is caused by endogenous secretion of
serotonin (chiefly) from carcinoid tumours.
The vast majority of patients with cardiac involvement present with
signs of right heart failure secondary to severe dysfunction of the
tricuspid and / or pulmonary valves.
The characteristic pathological findings of carcinoid heart disease are
endocardial plaques of fibrous tissue that may involve the tricuspid
valve, pulmonary valve, cardiac chambers, venae cavae, pulmonary
artery, and coronary sinus.
Sterile vegetations are associated with non-bacterial thrombotic
endocarditis (NBTE), formerly known as marantic endocarditis.
Infected platelet / fibrin deposits are associated with infective
endocarditis.
Annular dilatation is associated with 'functional' regurgitation caused by
a distorted or dilated ventricle, displacing the papillary muscles.
Calcification is related to age-related valve disease.
Carcinoid tumours
Carcinoid syndrome
usually occurs when metastases are present in the liver and release
serotonin into the systemic circulation
may also occur with lung carcinoid as mediators are not 'cleared' by
the liver
Features
flushing (often the earliest symptom)
diarrhoea
bronchospasm
hypotension
right heart valvular stenosis (left heart can be affected in bronchial
carcinoid)

This patient is a bar owner, and he is potentially under-estimating his
alcohol consumption. The chronic epigastric pain, weight loss and
diarrhoea are suggestive of malabsorption and this is likely to be related
to chronic pancreatitis and subsequent exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
Faecal elastase measurement is a direct indicator of the ability to
produce pancreatic enzymes. Normal elastase values are usually
considered to be greater than 200 mcg/g of stool, 100-200 may indicate
mild exocrine insufficiency, less than 100 is indicative of pancreatic
exocrine insufficiency.
Serum amylase is usually only usually elevated in episodes of acute
pancreatitis, it isn't therefore useful here. Faecal calprotectin is a
measure of GI tract inflammation, it's of value in evaluation of
inflammatory bowel disease, not in chronic pancreatitis. D-xylose
absorption testing is used to assess GI tract membrane integrity, and is
normal in patients with chronic pancreatitis. Anti-tissue
transglutaminase antibody testing is the screening test of choice for
coeliac disease. Although this is a cause of malabsorption, it isn't usually
a cause of epigastric pain.
Faecal elastase is the most useful initial investigation in patients
with possible chronic pancreatitis to determine exocrine pancreatic
insufficiency

inpatient with urinary sepsis. She is having 8-10 episodes per day of
watery, foul-smelling diarrhoea. Stool is sent for testing and Clostridium
difficile toxin is detected.
She is treated with a 10-day course of oral vancomycin. At the end of this
course, she describes no improvement and still has diarrhoea 8-10 times

What is the best course of action?

She is treated with a 10-day course of oral vancomycin. At the end of this
course, she describes no improvement and still has diarrhoea 8-10 times
per day. Observations are as follows.
Respiratory rate 18 /min
Oxygen saturations 97% on air
Heart rate 94 beats /min
Blood pressure 141/72mmHg
Temperature 38.1ºC
On examination, she appears dehydrated but the abdomen is soft and
non-tender. An abdominal X-ray is requested and is unremarkable.
What is the best course of action?
explanation:
If C. difficile does not respond to first-line vancomycin , oral
fidaxomicin should be used next, except in life-threatening
infections
The correct answer is switch to oral fidaxomicin. Vancomycin is
generally an effective first-line treatment but some patients may fail to
respond. In such cases, NICE recommends switching to oral fidaxomicin
for a 10-day course. In this case, the ongoing fever and the lack of
decrease in stool frequency suggest non-resolving infection rather than
other causes such as post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome.
Add IV metronidazole is incorrect. Oral vancomycin in combination with
IV metronidazole has a role in life-threatening infection or in
mild/moderate/severe infection that has not responded to first- or
second-line treatment. In the case described, there are no life-
threatening features and the patient has so far only received first-line
treatment.
Faecal microbiota transplant is incorrect. This is recommended as a
treatment option in recurrent Clostridium difficile infection where a
patient has 2 or more previous episodes. It is not recommended in acute
infection as in the case described.
Refer to general surgery is incorrect. Surgical management is only
warranted in the context of life-threatening infection. As above, there are
no features of life-threatening infection in the case described.
Switch to vancomycin enema is incorrect. Vancomycin via the
nasogastric or rectal route is only indicated if the oral route is not
available. In the case described, the patient's oral route is suitable and an
alternative oral treatment should be offered.

explanation:
Proton pump inhibitors have been associated with Clostridium difficile
infection and subsequent development of pseudomembranous colitis.
The clues to this diagnosis included the recent omeprazole use, foul
smelling diarrhoea, raised white cell count and abdominal film findings.
The patient is clearly unwell and will require adequate resuscitation
before further investigation to confirm the diagnosis.
Diverticulitis can present with abdominal pain and diarrhoea but the clue
here is the profuse foul smelling diarrhoea characteristic of Clostridium
difficile infection.
Salmonellosis is unlikely as there is nothing from the history to suggest
exposure to the bacterium.
Ischaemic colitis typically presents in the elderly with abdominal pain
and often bloody diarrhoea.
Inflammatory bowel disease can present similarly but one would expect
to have seen a change in bowel habit prior to this acute episode.
PPIs are a risk factor for C. difficile infection

of classical 'bronze diabetes': diabetes, skin pigmentation and liver
cirrhosis. The clinical picture is supported by the elevated ferritin levels
and elevated transferrin saturation. The diagnosis is confirmed by the
patient being homozygous for the C282Y mutation of the HFE gene on
chromosome 6 (the most common genotype associated with iron
overload). The patient would also require additional investigation to

echocardiography and liver biopsy or liver MRI.

haemochromatosis and is indicated in all patients with a ferritin level
greater than 1,000 microgram / L. Typical initial phlebotomy regimes are
400-500 ml every 1-2 weeks. Once ferritin level falls to the range 50-100

schedule every 2-4 months. Please note, that the incorrect answer of

(1:80) which is non-specific and commonly encountered in patients with

hepatitis (smooth muscle, LKM1 and soluble liver antigen) are all
negative, making this diagnosis less likely.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is incorrect. We would expect an
obstructive pattern of LFT derangement in this case.
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is now the most common
cause of liver disease in the developed world. It is largely caused by
obesity and describes a spectrum of disease ranging from:
steatosis - fat in the liver
steatohepatitis - fat with inflammation, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis
(NASH), see below
progressive disease may cause fibrosis and liver cirrhosis
NAFLD is thought to represent the hepatic manifestation of the
metabolic syndrome and hence insulin resistance is thought to be the
key mechanism leading to steatosis.
Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a term used to describe liver
changes similar to those seen in alcoholic hepatitis in the absence of a
history of alcohol abuse. It is relatively common and thought to affect
around 3-4% of the general population. The progression of disease in
patients with NASH may be responsible for a proportion of patients
previously labelled as cryptogenic cirrhosis.
Associated factors
obesity
type 2 diabetes mellitus
hyperlipidaemia

explanation:
This patient has fatigue, generalised itching, elevated bilirubin, alkaline
phosphatase, and slightly elevated aminotransferases, suggesting a
diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). PBC is the slow,
progressive autoimmune destruction of the bile ducts, leading to biliary
stasis, hyperbilirubinemia, and pruritus. Antimitochondrial antibodies are
highly specific for this condition. Antinuclear antibodies are often
positive in autoimmune conditions and are not specific to PBC.
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medication for primary biliary
cholangitis. It slows down the progression of PBC and provides relief for
symptoms like itching.
Budesonide is given to patients with some immunological disorders,
such as autoimmune hepatitis. Patients with autoimmune hepatitis will
have typical features like weight loss, abdominal pain, anti-smooth
muscle antibodies, and hypergammaglobulinaemia. Autoimmune
hepatitis is also not usually associated with a positive antimitochondrial
antibody.
Cholestyramine is used in patients with hypercholesterolemia. It can
also provide symptomatic relief in itching secondary to cholestatic
disease like PBC. Although cholestyramine could help relieve itching in
this patient, it would not slow disease progression. It is not the first-line
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medication for primary biliary
cholangitis
management for this patient's condition.
A liver biopsy may be needed for the diagnosis and management of
several hepatic and biliary conditions. It is indicated only if PBC is
suspected but ambiguous or if there is no response to treatment. This
patient has a clear diagnosis of PBC and should start therapy.
A liver transplant is indicated in the cases of PBC only when bilirubin
levels rise above 100 µmol/l.
Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis (previously referred to as primary biliary
cirrhosis) is a chronic liver disorder typically seen in middle-aged
females (female:male ratio of 9:1). The aetiology is not fully understood
although it is thought to be an autoimmune condition. Interlobular bile
ducts become damaged by a chronic inflammatory process causing
progressive cholestasis which may eventually progress to cirrhosis. The
classic presentation is itching in a middle-aged woman
Associations
Sjogren's syndrome (seen in up to 80% of patients)
rheumatoid arthritis
systemic sclerosis
thyroid disease

early: may be asymptomatic (e.g. raised ALP on routine LFTs) or
fatigue, pruritus
cholestatic jaundice
hyperpigmentation, especially over pressure points
around 10% of patients have right upper quadrant pain

options: High calcium, high phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase
Low calcium, high phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase
Low calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase
Normal calcium, normal phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase
Normal calcium, normal phosphate, normal alkaline phosphatase
explanation:
The scenario here is most likely to be vitamin D deficiency, presenting
with osteomalacia. The patient has a number of risk factors - his age,
and being housebound and thus not receiving any sunlight exposure.
The symptoms and examination findings support the likely diagnosis of
vitamin D deficiency. With this deficiency, calcium is therefore low,
phosphate is also low, and alkaline phosphatase is usually raised.
In Vitamin D deficiency, there is usually low serum calcium, low
serum phosphate and high serum alkaline phosphatase
High calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase is not referring to
any specific pathology.
Low calcium, high phosphate and high alkaline phosphatase refers to
secondary hyperparathyroidism. Whilst this is often due to vitamin D
deficiency as well, the primary findings in the scenario above are those
of osteomalacia.
Normal calcium, normal phosphate and high alkaline phosphatase is
suggestive of Paget's disease. This would also present with bone pain,
but may also lead to vision and hearing problems as skull bone thickens.
Given that the history above mentions being housebound and a lack of
sunlight exposure, as well as proximal weakness and waddling gait,
osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency is more likely.
Normal calcium, normal phosphate and normal alkaline phosphatase
may be seen in osteopenia, where bone mineral density is low. The
history above is more suggestive of osteomalacia.

The correct answer for this question is pancreatic cancer.
Courvoisier's sign states that in a patient with a painless, enlarged
gallbladder and mild jaundice the cause is unlikely to be gallstones.
Furthermore, it is more likely to be a malignancy of the pancreas or
biliary tree.
Alcoholic hepatitis and primary biliary cirrhosis are a reasonable
differentials. However, an examination finding of a painless, enlarged
gallbladder makes both of these differentials less likely.
The scenario does not suggest paracetamol overdose, as this would not
cause a painless, palpable gallbladder. Furthermore, jaundice is not
usually seen in paracetamol overdose.
Pancreatic cancer
Pancreatic cancer is often diagnosed late as it tends to present in a non-
specific way. Over 80% of pancreatic tumours are adenocarcinomas
which typically occur at the head of the pancreas.

Question 57 of 267
A 22-year-old man presents with a tremor and the feeling of 'slowing
down'. Lately, the patient has noticed that he is feeling more nauseated,
has pain in his abdomen, worse around the right upper quadrant. His
friends have commented that his eyes have changed colour and are
turning yellow.
Which investigation result is most supportive of a diagnosis of Wilson's?
explanation:
The correct answer is elevated 24-hour urinary copper excretion. Whilst
serum copper and serum ceruloplasmin levels are useful in the
diagnosis of Wilson's disease they are expected to be lowered rather
than elevated. It would be very likely that the transaminases would be
elevated in this patient as he has right upper quadrant pain and jaundice,
but this is not specific for Wilson's disease. It would be unlikely that
hepatic function would be sufficiently impaired to affect pro-thrombin
time for this patient, and even if this was the case it is not specific for
Wilson's disease.

explanation:

and examination findings mean variceal bleeding should be suspected.
This patient should therefore be managed as an acute upper GI variceal
bleed according to NICE guidelines (updated August 2016) and receive
terlipressin and broad spectrum antibiotics. Platelets are indicated as
count is below 50 and FFP is indicated due to raised INR/APTT > 1.5 x
normal. Cryoprecipitate is only required if fibrinogen remains below 1.5
after FFP. Red cell transfusion should follow local guidelines but with
Hb>100 is certainly not indicated at this stage.
Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding
Acute upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a common and important
presentation. It may be caused by a wide variety of conditions but is
most commonly due to either oesophageal varices or peptic ulcer
disease.

haematemesis
the most common presenting feature
often bright red but may sometimes be described as 'coffee

melena

The correct answer is a proton pump inhibitor, metronidazole and
clarithromycin. This is a patient with a peptic ulcer associated with
Helicobacter pylori. NICE advises an eradication strategy, which should
take allergies and recent antibiotic use into account.
FIrst-line treatment over seven days:
If no allergies: PPI, amoxicillin and clarithromycin or metronidazole
If penicillin allergic: PPI, clarithromycin and metronidazole
If penicillin allergic and previous clarithromycin exposure: PP,
bismuth, metronidazole and tetracycline
As he may be penicillin allergic he should be treated as per the second
option.

'Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease and Dyspepsia in Adults:
Investigation and Management.' Clinical Guideline [CG184]. The National
Institute for Health and Care Excellence, Nov. 2014.
Helicobacter pylori
Helicobacter pylori is a Gram-negative bacteria associated with a variety
of gastrointestinal problems, principally peptic ulcer disease.

A 28-year-old man with newly-diagnosed distal ulcerative colitis is seen
in the gastroenterology clinic for a follow-up appointment. He was last
seen 4 weeks earlier with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea and
reported opening his bowels about 5 times a day without fever or
vomiting. He was started on rectal mesalazine.
On return to the clinic this afternoon, he reports that his symptoms have
remained the same and his bowels are still opening 4-5 times a day with
cramping abdominal pain.
His observations are as follows:
Temperature 37.2ºC
Heart rate 88bpm
Blood pressure 124/77mmHg
Respiratory rate 14 breaths/min
Oxygen saturations 99% on air
On examination, his abdomen is soft but mildly tender in the left iliac
fossa. His cardiovascular examination is unremarkable.
What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
The patient has been having a moderate ulcerative colitis flare with 4-6
episodes of bloody stools per day without any systemic symptoms.
Having a diagnosis of distal ulcerative colitis means that rectal
aminosalicylates can be used initially, such as rectal mesalazine. NICE
guidelines recommend that if patients with distal ulcerative colitis do not
respond to topical medication within 4 weeks an oral aminosalicylate
should be tried, making oral mesalazine the correct answer.
Intravenous hydrocortisone is reserved for acute, severe flares of
ulcerative colitis that are associated with systemic upset and warrant
hospital admission.
Azathioprine is a drug used to maintain remission in Crohn's disease
and ulcerative colitis. As this patient is not yet in remission and is still
experiencing symptoms, it would be inappropriate to start treatment.
Oral metronidazole is used in the treatment of rectal and fistulating
Crohn's disease. It is not used in the treatment of ulcerative colitis.
Topical corticosteroids can be tried in the treatment of distal ulcerative
colitis. However, their indication is following unsuccessful remission
with oral aminosalicylate use.

explanation:
The diagnosis of the underlying cause of anaemia is in the blood film:
the patient has Heinz bodies, small inclusion bodies in red blood cells
that are a consequence of usually oxidative damage to haemoglobin
components. Note the close temporal association of the anaemia with
starting sulphasalazine. Drugs such as sulphasalazine, dapsone,
ribavirin and poisoning with paraquat ingestion leads to the oxidation of
Fe2+ (ferrous) components of haem to Fe3+ (ferric), forming
methaemoglobin. When the intrinsic antioxidation mechanism of
NADPH and glutathione is overwhelmed, red cell components undergo
oxidative damage and cell death, leading to haemolysis, explaining the
significantly raised LDH. Methaemoglobin is converted to hemichromes
and eventually precipitated to Heinz bodies.
The treatment of oxidative haemolytic anaemia is by withdrawal of the
offending drug alone. There is no role for steroids in this setting: the
symptoms are not consistent with an ulcerative colitis flare. Blood
abnormalities should normalise within weeks of drug withdrawal:
transfusion of further red blood cells prior to stopping the drug would
only result in further haemolysis.
Aminosalicylate drugs
5-aminosalicyclic acid (5-ASA) is released in the colon and is not
absorbed. It acts locally as an anti-inflammatory. The mechanism of
action is not fully understood but 5-ASA may inhibit prostaglandin
synthesis

explanation:
The patient has presented with features of small bowel obstruction,
namely the abdominal pain which is relieved by vomiting. It is important
to remember that abdominal distension may be absent in small bowel
obstruction (SBO). The most common cause of SBO is intra-abdominal
adhesions, accounting for the majority of cases, followed by hernias and
inflammatory structures (e.g. Crohn disease). Rarer causes include
gallstone ileus.
The past medical history of recurrent cholecystitis, evidence of
pneumobilia (air in the biliary tree), and the presence of SBO makes
gallstone ileus the most likely unifying diagnosis. Gallstone ileus is an
uncommon cause of a mechanical small bowel obstruction. It is a rare
complication of chronic cholecystitis and occurs when a gallstone
passes through a fistula between the gallbladder and small bowel before
becoming impacted at the ileocaecal valve.
The amylase is only mildly raised and certainly not high enough to be
diagnostic of pancreatitis. It is important to remember that amylase is
non-specific and can be raised due to a variety of processes. Although
pancreatitis can cause a sentinel loop, which is a short segment of
adynamic ileus close to an intra-abdominal inflammatory process, it
would not cause a small bowel obstruction.
A paraduodenal abscess and emphysematous cholangitis can also
cause pneumobilia, however they would not result in small bowel
obstruction, making gall stone ileus a better answer.
Gallstone ileus is a mechanical small bowel obstruction which
occurs due a gallstone obstruction most often in the ileum

demonstrated by ongoing diarrhoea and persisting detectable toxin in
the stool. The 3rd line option to treat the infection in this circumstance is
oral vancomycin +/- IV metronidazole.
Colectomy is incorrect. This option would only be used in the setting of
life-threatening disease. There is no documentation to suggest that is
the case here.
Faecal transplant is incorrect. While this is an option for treating
recurrent Clostridium difficile infection, it is only used after more
conservative measures have been exhausted.
IV vancomycin is incorrect. This method of administering vancomycin is
ineffective in Clostridium difficile infection and should not be used.
If a first episode of C. difficile doesn't respond to either vancomycin
or fidaxomicin then oral vancomycin +/- IV metronidazole should be
tried
Repeat oral fidaxomicin is incorrect. Repeating a course of oral
vancomycin rather than fidaxomicin is a recognized option.
Clostridioides difficile
Clostridioides difficile is a Gram positive rod often encountered in
hospital practice. It produces an exotoxin which causes intestinal
damage leading to a syndrome called pseudomembranous colitis. C.
difficile develops when the normal gut flora are suppressed by broad-
spectrum antibiotics. Clindamycin is historically associated with causing
C. difficile but the aetiology has evolved significantly over the past 10
years. Second and third-generation cephalosporins are now the leading
cause of C. difficile.
Other than antibiotics, risk factors include:
proton pump inhibitors
Pathophysiology
anaerobic gram-positive, spore-forming, toxin-producing bacillus
transmission: via the faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores
releases two exotoxins (toxin A and toxin B) that act on intestinal
epithelial cells and inflammatory cells resulting in colitis
Features
diarrhoea
abdominal pain
a raised white blood cell count (WCC) is characteristic
if severe toxic megacolon may develop
The Public Health England severity scale is often used as this may
determine treatment:

affect both the exocrine and endocrine functions of the pancreas.

The patient in the scenario is experiencing malabsorption following
bowel resection. The presentation and blood test results don't suggest a
flare of her Crohn's disease and so alternate diagnoses should be
sought. Having an ileal resection predisposes patients to malabsorption
syndromes, particularly bile salt malabsorption, leading to persistent

Oral mesalazine is used in the treatment of Crohn's disease, such as
mild flares. The normal blood test results do not suggest a flare and
therefore this answer is incorrect.

gastrointestinal infections, such as Clostridioides difficile or giardiasis.
There is no suggestion of these infections from the history, therefore this
answer is incorrect.
Prednisolone may be used in flares of Crohn's disease, however, the
normal blood test results mean this diagnosis is less likely. Therefore,
both oral prednisolone and rectal prednisolone are incorrect.

explanation:
This lady has severe active Crohn's disease, and she is on day 5 of
treatment with IV hydrocortisone with no improvement of symptoms.
The next step in management should be considered, which would be
Biologic therapy is considered in treatment of an acute flare of
Crohn's disease when symptoms don't improve after 5 days of IV
hydrocortisone
anti-TNFα agents e.g. infliximab or adalimumab.

children or young people where there are concerns about growth or side
effects of treatment.
Rectal mesalazine is more often used in the management of ulcerative
colitis, rather than Crohn's disease.

jaundice. This has come on suddenly in the last few days. The patient
denies any excessive alcohol consumption drinking only the occasional

recurrent urinary tract infections. This has been managed in the
community with once daily prophylactic antibiotics.
Liver function tests reveal:
Total bilirubin
74 µmol/l
Unconjugated bilirubin
35 µmol/l
Conjugated bilirubin
39 µmol/l
ALP
110 u/l
AST
219 u/l
What is the most likely causative agent for these results?
explanation:
The results above represent a hepatocellular cause of jaundice. This is
shown from the elevated unconjugated bilirubin levels and differentiates
it from a post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice. All of the agents above can
cause a cholestatic (obstructive) picture but the most likely cause of a
hepatocellular jaundice is nitrofurantoin. This occurs with chronic use of
the medication. It is associated with hepatic necrosis and should be
stopped immediately when there is any evidence of hepatic necrosis.
The side effects of nitrofurantoin can be fatal and as such attention
must be paid to its appearance on a drug history. Toxic effects can
manifest as hepatic disease as shown here but also as both an acute
and chronic respiratory condition, agranulocytosis and the acute
hypersensitivity reaction of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.
There is no clear guidance in the use of antibiotic prophylaxis in adult
patients. However, recent Cochrane review questioned the use in
children. The other common advice given to patients is to drink
cranberry juice to prevent further infections, but this again has not been
backed up by the study data. Therefore there is currently no consensus,
but recurrent UTI should warrant further investigations by either a
gynaecologist or urologist in adults and most certainly a paediatrician in
children.
Drug-induced liver disease
Drug-induced liver disease is generally divided into hepatocellular,
cholestatic or mixed. There is however considerable overlap, with some
drugs causing a range of changes to the liver
The following drugs tend to cause a hepatocellular picture:
paracetamol
sodium valproate, phenytoin
MAOIs
halothane
anti-tuberculosis: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide
statins
alcohol
amiodarone
methyldopa
nitrofurantoin

This man is suffering from septic shock and end-organ damage
secondary to the hypoperfusion. This is evidenced by the deranged LFTs
and AKI. Therefore ischaemic hepatitis is the most likely diagnosis.
Co-amoxiclav is known to cause cholestatic liver injury. If this was the
cause, the ALP would be proportionally higher compared to the ALT.
There is no question that the patient is septic with the presentation of
fever, tachycardia, hypotension and raised inflammatory markers.
However, there is no evidence of abdominal pain; and the symptoms and
x-ray finding are in keeping with community-acquired pneumonia
therefore biliary sepsis is not the most likely cause.
Alcoholic hepatitis would be associated with a greater increase in
bilirubin. There is also no evidence provided to support alcohol misuse.
Whilst we know that patient had been taking paracetamol, there are no
details indicating overdose. In these situations, it would be good practice
to check paracetamol levels.
Acute hypoperfusion (e.g. low BP secondary to blood loss) may
result in ischaemic hepatitis
Ischaemic hepatitis
Ischaemic hepatitis is a diffuse hepatic injury resulting from acute
hypoperfusion (sometimes known as 'shock liver'). It is not an
inflammatory process. It is diagnosed in the presence of an inciting
event (e.g. a cardiac arrest) and marked increases in aminotransferase
levels (exceeding 1000 international unit/L or 50 times the upper limit of
normal). Often, it will occur in conjunction with acute kidney injury
(tubular necrosis) or other end-organ dysfunction.

explanation:
This patient has bile acid malabsorption following extensive terminal
ileal and small bowel resection for his Crohn's disease. A complication
of extensive terminal ileal resection is bile acid diarrhoea which presents
with watery loose stools including nocturnal episodes. The diagnostic
test is the SeHCAT scan (nuclear medicine) which used radiolabelled
selenium and measures the retention of the labelled molecule. BAD is
diagnosed by a <15% retention of SeHCAT at 7 days.
The treatment is with bile acid sequestrants including cholestyramine
(Questran). This is the correct answer here, the patient does not have an
acute flare so Infliximab frequency does not need altering. Loperamide
and codeine will not treat the underlying cause and octreotide can be
used to treat diarrhoea in VIPomas.
Ongoing diarrhoea in Crohn's patient post-resection with normal
CRP → cholestyramine
Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant used in the management of
hyperlipidaemia. It decreases bile acid reabsorption in the small
intestine, therefore upregulating the amount of cholesterol that is
converted to bile acid. The main effect it has on the lipid profile is to
reduce LDL cholesterol. It is also occasionally used in Crohn's disease
for treatment diarrhoea following bowel resection.
Adverse effects
abdominal cramps and constipation
decreases absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
cholesterol gallstones
may raise level of triglycerides

there is evidence of active disease. Adalimumab can be used as an
alternative.

Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis (previously referred to as primary biliary
cirrhosis) is a chronic liver disorder typically seen in middle-aged
females (female:male ratio of 9:1). The aetiology is not fully understood
although it is thought to be an autoimmune condition. Interlobular bile
ducts become damaged by a chronic inflammatory process causing
progressive cholestasis which may eventually progress to cirrhosis. The
classic presentation is itching in a middle-aged woman

options: Urea and electrolytes, including phosphate and magnesium
explanation:
Alcoholic patients are often malnourished. In hospital the patient has
(hopefully!) no access to alcohol but also three meals a day provided.
Re-feeding syndrome is the only condition responsible for the above
symptoms that can be readily diagnosed from the above tests. Blood
tests will reveal electrolyte disturbances particularly hypophsphataemia
accompanying the neurological and pulmonary manifestations.
Treatment involves replacing the depleted electrolytes and slow build up
of diet.

Question 78 of 267
A 49-year-old man with a history of alcoholism has been admitted to the
ward for a detoxification program. He was brought to the hospital by
police in an intoxicated state. He has been treated with B vitamin
replacement therapy and has now begun re-feeding. You are asked to
see him because of acute shortness of breath and generalised muscle
weakness. On examination his blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg, pulse is
86 beats per minute and regular. He has bilateral crackles on
auscultation of his chest consistent with heart failure, and global 4/5
power weakness.
Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Globalised muscle weakness coupled with symptoms of heart failure is
consistent with re-feeding syndrome. This occurs because of intra-
cellular movement of phosphate, thought to be related to be related to
hyperinsulinaemia because of carbohydrate loading. Heart failure and
muscle weakness can be avoided by ensuring that any feeds used
contain adequate phosphate when used in the treatment of patients at
risk of re-feeding syndrome, such as those with alcoholism and / or
eating disorders.
Low thiamine results in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Although low
potassium can result in muscle weakness and is seen in reactive
hyperinsulinaemia, feeds normally contain adequate potassium to avoid
this, hence it's less likely than hypophosphataemia in this situation.
Folate deficiency is manifest by anaemia, glossitis, and neuropathy, and
magnesium deficiency presents with similar symptoms to
hypocalcaemia.
Refeeding syndrome
Refeeding syndrome describes the metabolic abnormalities which occur
on feeding a person following a period of starvation. It occurs when an
extended period of catabolism ends abruptly with switching to
carbohydrate metabolism. The metabolic consequences include:
hypophosphataemia
this is the hallmark symptom of refeeding syndrome
may result in significant muscle weakness, including
myocardial muscle (→ cardiac failure) and the diaphragm (→
respiratory failure)
hypokalaemia
hypomagnesaemia: may predispose to torsades de pointes
abnormal fluid balance
Pathophysiology of Hypophosphatemia in Refeeding Syndrome:
Shift from Fat to Carbohydrate Metabolism: In refeeding syndrome,
the reintroduction of carbohydrates leads to a shift from fat to
carbohydrate metabolism. This switch activates insulin secretion,
which in turn increases cellular uptake of glucose.

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is now the most common
cause of liver disease in the developed world. It is largely caused by
obesity and describes a spectrum of disease ranging from:

progressive disease may cause fibrosis and liver cirrhosis

metabolic syndrome and hence insulin resistance is thought to be the
key mechanism leading to steatosis.

You review a 30-year-old male who was seen in the gastroenterology
department with a first presentation of ulcerative colitis symptoms He
was having diarrhoea 5 times a day with small amount of blood in his
stool. He had been systemically well and haemodynamically stable and
thus did not require hospital admission. He was started on daily
Pentasa.
Today, he reports his symptoms have not improved despite treatment.
He is still opening his bowels 5 times per day and is concern about it.
He is mildly dehydrated clinically, but haemodynamically stable, with a
blood pressure of 120/76 mmHg and a heart rate of 70 beats per
minute. His abdomen is soft and not distended.
What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
This gentleman has symptoms of moderate ulcerative colitis which was
not managed with oral 5 ASA. He is not on topical therapy following an
initial assessment which gives you the clue that his disease is not
isolated to proctitis.
His symptoms are still that of moderate ulcerative colitis and given his
failure to respond to treatment he should now be started on oral
prednisolone with a follow up in 2 weeks for re-review of symptoms.
Mild to moderate ulcerative colitis ( up to 6 motions per day with mild
bleed. ESR <30) should be managed using a stepwise approach.
Proctitis: Induce remission with a topical 5-ASA (aminosalicylic
acid). If no response or cant tolerate, 5-ASA the next step would be
to add topical steroids. Oral should be considered if remission not
achieved or patient presents with left-sided extensive ulcerative
colitis.
Left-sided extensive disease should be managed using oral 5-ASA
initially with or without topical 5-ASA. If no improvement within 4
weeks oral prednisolone therapy should be added. If no response to
oral prednisolone, tacrolimus should be started to induce remission.

transfusion, endoscopy or surgery.

agents they should be held too.
Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding
Acute upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a common and important
presentation. It may be caused by a wide variety of conditions but is
most commonly due to either oesophageal varices or peptic ulcer
disease.

A 55-year-old man attends the emergency department following a
collapse at a family barbecue. Prior to the collapse, he complained of
feeling dizzy with a fluttering feeling in his chest. He has a past medical
history of hypertension for which he takes amlodipine and ramipril.
On examination, he is alert and oriented. Peripheral pulses are intact
bilaterally and his lying and standing blood pressures are 155/89mmHg
and 147/80mmHg, respectively. On auscultation, his chest is clear and
heart sounds are normal. His neurological examination is unremarkable,
although he still complains of feeling dizzy.
An ECG is taken, as shown below:
© Image used on license from Dr Smith, University of Minnesota
What is the next most immediate step in the management of this
patient?
explanation:
This patient's ECG shows peaked T waves and QRS widening in the
majority of the leads in keeping with hyperkalaemia. Additional ECG
findings include P wave flattening, PR interval prolongation, conduction
blocks and bradyarrhythmias. Hyperkalaemia can cause collapse and
dizziness as experienced by this patient. Furthermore, the medication
history of ramipril puts this patient at a higher risk of developing
hyperkalaemia. The treatment of choice is an infusion of calcium
gluconate to stabilise the cardiac membrane.
Amiodarone is used in the treatment of tachyarrhythmias including atrial
fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia. Whilst this patient's ECG features
broad QRS complexes, this patient is not tachycardic with a heart rate of
around 66bpm. Furthermore, the significantly peaked T waves are not
suggestive of a tachyarrhythmia. Rather, they indicate hyperkalaemia.
Synchronised electrical cardioversion is used in the management of
tachyarrhythmias with adverse features (e.g. shock, myocardial
ischaemia, heart failure). Not only does this patient's ECG not represent
a tachyarrhythmia, but there are also no adverse features at present and
this patient is haemodynamically stable.
Transcutaneous pacing would be indicated if this patient's ECG
demonstrated a bradyarrhythmia, particularly one with a significant risk
factor for asystole (e.g. Mobitz type II or complete heart block). It does
not play a role in the treatment of hyperkalaemia.
Although there is an ambiguous QRS morphology on this patient's ECG,
there is no clear ST-segment elevation. Instead, there are significantly
peaked T waves that may give a false impression of ST-segment
elevation. With this in mind, it is unlikely that this patient would benefit
from primary percutaneous coronary intervention.

hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) but evidence of efficacy in patients without
HRS is lacking.

additional benefit over treatment with prednisolone alone, whilst the use
of N-acetylcysteine as monotherapy in alcoholic hepatitis is not
recommended. In one randomised controlled trial, combination therapy
with prednisolone and N-acetylcysteine was shown to be superior to
prednisolone monotherapy in reducing mortality at 28 days; largely due

His observations are as follows: blood pressure 130/66mmHg, heart
